speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, February 16, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are considering
item 1.

Will the minister tell us
the bearing of the amendments to the order in council referred to yesterday?
I have not had an opportunity to look that up. I will have it put in hand to be looked up.

What I complain of is
that the amendments to the army regulations, by virtue of the mobilization act, are not, I would say, self-supporting. They refer to other pieces of legislation which are not included in the draft of these amendments. I have one here, P.C. 9372 of December 7, amending PC. 7989 of October 14, 1943. It refers to the N.SjS. mobilization act regulations and changes section 26. What I complain of further is the drafting of section 26 in the original order in council, P.C. 7989. It reads:
A man reporting at a centre in consequence of an order-military training or who has been taken thereto in consequence of an order made pursuant to section 28 (1) N.S.S. mobilization regulations shall, until such time as he is enrolled or shall have been dispatched to his destination be deemed to be a person as is mentioned in subsection 10 of section 176 of the Army Act, not otherwise subject to military law, who is a follower of or accompanies His Majesty's troops or any portion thereof when employed on active service. The Army Act, to the extent that it forms part of the law of Canada, shall apply to such a man, and he shall be subject to military law' accordingly. Such a man shall be deemed to be under the command of the officer commanding the centre, provided always, however, that, notwithstanding the provisions of subsection 2 of section 184 of the said Army Act, such a man may be punished by such commanding officer in like manner and to the same extent as if he were a private soldier serving on active service under the command of that officer.
It is dated December 7 of last year. Who understands a word of it? No one. Here is the Army Act referred to in that order in council. Let me quote two sections of it. The minister knows better than anyone else that the Army Act is a piece of English legislation that dates back more than half a century. The first reference is to subsection 10, the definition of "person". Subsection 10 of section 176 reads:
All persons not otherwise subject to military law who are follow'ers of or accompany His Majesty's troops or any portion thereof, when employed on active service, subject to this qualification, that, where any such persons are employed by or are followers of or accompany any portion of His Majesty's forces, consisting partly of His Majesty's Indian forces subject to Indian military law, or consisting partly of His Majesty's Burma forces subject to Burma

military law, and such persons are natives of India, or as the case may be, natives of Burma they shall be subject to the Indian military law or, as the case may be, to Burma military law.
In the amendment it is specified that that section applies to the Canadian order in council in so far as it is possible. It would be absurd to suggest that our men should be subject to the Indian law or the Burma law.
Here is subsection 2 of section 184 of the Army Act, which in my opinion is very bad drafting:
Any person subject to military law who does not belong to His Majesty's forces shall, for the purposes of this act relating to offences, be deemed to be under the command of the commanding officer of the corps or portion of a corps (if any) to which he is attached, and if he is not attached to any corps or a portion of a corps under the command of any officer who may for the time being be named as his commanding officer, by the general or other officer commanding the force with which such person may for the time being be, or of any other prescribed officer, or. if no such officer is named or prescribed, under the command of the said general or other officer commanding, but such person shall not be liable to be punished by a commanding officer:	provided
that a general or other officer commanding shall not place a person under the command of an officer of rank inferior to the official rank of such person is there is present, at the place where such person is, any officer of higher rank under whose command he can be placed.
If anyone understands that, he deserves a reward. Let me summarize my point in this way. This is very bad legislation, very bad drafting, but it will be accepted by the Tory party at once. A very clever man once told me it is sufficient to say that it comes from the British war office and the Tories will adopt it at once. They will adopt it without question provided it comes from the B.W.O. It was ever thus. How is it that the bright brains of the judge advocate general's branch cannot draft legislation for this country without reference to such legal instruments? That kind of legislation has a purpose. It is similar to the plebiscite question, a question that was understood by none and which could be inter-[DOT]preted in many ways. It is nebulous. It is purposely foggy and nebulous. I want something clear. It seems to me it is reasonable to press for clear legislation, legislation that is complete and understandable. One should not have to go over all the shelves of the library to find out the meaning.
Now sir, there are some points that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee. It is impossible to carry on an orderly discussion without clear legislation; but I try to speak in the plainest possible English in order to be understood by all. Hon.

members have the right to agree or disagree with me, but I want my colleagues at least to understand the point I am trying to make. I said yesterday that if the army is given priority over essential industry, national selective service is through. We have heard a lot about essential industry. Some time ago, last year or the year before, the Minister of National Defence said that he tried to urge the employer to replace men in essenfial industry by men who are unfit, and even by women, to release men for the army. I deny that the army is the only essential industry. I am not opposed to the army. There is no one who tries to do more to help the returned man, to help those who are in the army, who looks after them, who listens to them, who has the honour of their confidence when they come to him, than I. It is precisely for the underdog, for the one who has not the right, to call upon his superior officer to speak about his grievances, that I act now. I do it in order that we may have a well-balanced war effort in this country. The idea of the imperialist Tories is to see a soldier without uniform, without shoes, without food, without weapons and without ammunition, who would swim across the Atlantic and then find some Irish confetti on Irish soil to fight the enemy. There would be no clothes for him, no transportation, no food, no arms and no ammunition for him. That is the ideal state of the soldier as seen by the Simon-pure imperialist Tories. Is it not absurd?
There has been a decrease of thirteen billion dollars in the estimates of the United States army. We have a reduction of about two hundred million. But there are very strange things happening. If anyone happens to go to the central station of the Canadain National Railways in Montreal he will see a plate inscribed with the number 17,035. That is the number of men connected with the railway, who have enlisted-men from an essential industry, carrying passengers, military and civil, food and ammunition throughout the country; and I am informed the number now is 21,000; twenty-one thousand experienced men who have been taken from an essential industry and placed in the army, and the army is not yet satisfied. What, has been done? I want to have complete information, not only from the Minister of National Defence, but also from the Minister of Labour, as to the understanding that has taken place between the army and the Canadian National Railways regarding the appointment of a man named Edge, who was promoted from superintendent of personnel to the fat job of director of labour relations, and without whose signature a man who has not had ten or more years' experience has to join the colours if he has

War Appropriation-Army
been in a training camp for a month. What happened? To my personal knowledge officials of the railway who are right there on the spot in the division, who know the work of all the men in key positions of the railway, on the trains as operators, certify that the men are essential to the railway; but this man in Montreal, who does not answer any letters, keeps all these recommendations from responsible officials on his desk. Because he does so, because that single man, who is well paid for it, does not return the application for an extension of leave for the men to military headquarters, it is said that the men have filed no application for extension of leave and therefore they have to join the army. There is another man who does the same job on the Canadian Pacific Railway. If we are to have total war as preached by the jingoes and as preached by some other people, I will agree with them, provided that the war effort is well balanced, and provided that the soldier can rely upon the help of essential industry and of men who have particular experience in certain key positions in essential industry. I do not take this stand because we are against the war effort; not at all. I. take the stand because we want the war effort to be well balanced. We want everybody to do his very best in the successful prosecution of the war. My contention is that a man with years of experience on the railway is doing more for the war effort by continuing to work on the railway than he would by going into the army, for which he has no technical experience. The man at the throttle of his locomotive, the fireman, the brakeman or the conductor, can better help his country along the road to victory by continuing in that work than by going into the army as a private, a non-commissioned officer or an officer. That is my point. I have some cases to bring to the attention of the minister. I shall not mention them now, because it would take too long, but I shall write his parliamentary assistant and give each case.
I want this system changed; I want a decentralization of this control in connection with the railways. Is not the local superintendent in each part of the country, each division, in a better position than one man in Montreal to say that Tom or Joe or Jim is essential to the railway business? The understanding between the army and the railways has gone so far that the divisional superintendents have been notified by Mr. Edge in Montreal that in future they are not to recommend anyone for postponement, that all men who have had a month's training, whatever may have been their experience on the railway, were bound to go back to the 100-374
army and become soldiers. Why speak of selective service after that? If that is not disguised conscription, if it is not sabotage of our war effort, what is it? It is just as clear as spring water that it is going to have a disastrous effect. These men who are in good health, and who have had enough experience to hold these responsible positions, cannot be replaced on the railways by new men unfit for military sendee.
Last year, in the Hong Kong debate, thirty-four hon. members voted for reform in the Department of National Defence, while ten others who were paired said that if they had voted they would have supported the motion, meaning that in their opinion reform was needed in the department. It is all right to allow the department the number of men that essential industry can dispense with, but on the other hand it would prove most disastrous to this country if essential industry were disorganized in order to have more men in the army. I hope that in the course of this discussion the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Labour will give a full explanation as to the understanding that has been arrived at between the army and our two great railways, and also as to what has been done by selective service in regard to the appointment of Mr. Edge and the gentleman who occupies the same position' with the Canadian Pacific Railway company.
That having been said, and my time being short, I cannot allow to pass unnoticed the dispatch that appeared in today's newspapers from the pen of Mr. Shapiro. Yesterday I said I could not understand why just a few hon. members had been called in by the government to be informed as to the correspondence exchanged in regard to the resignation of Lieutenant-General McNaugh-ton. I will ask the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services to speak behind the curtain if they are not interested in what is being said in the house. Frequently at the opening of the house, on the order for motions or on the orders of the day, a minister makes a reservation in connection with the adoption of a motion for papers by a private member. Every time that happens, some hon. members opposite, particularly the leader of the opposition and the leaders of the other groups, protest and ask how it is that the minister should be able to make his own reservations, since we are entitled to know everything. That is a democratic stand. But how can they say they are being logical with themselves-and I speak of all of them now-when they meet together to discuss matters in which we are all interested, and as to which we might be all
War Appropriation-Army

informed in a secret sitting? And how is it that we cannot be told here in Ottawa what is published in London and the press of this continent? It could not be told to members of parliament yesterday. It appeared this morning in all the Canadian papers. Is it not an anomaly?
There is more to it than that. If something secret comes up at a meeting of cabinet council in the east block, it must be for the members of the cabinet alone; if I am well informed they take an oath to keep all matters secret, in regard to what happens behind those doors. Then how is it that the leader of the official opposition should be called in by the government, to be told in confidence things that cannot be told to other hon. members?
An hon. MEMBEK: Union government.
Mr. POULIOT; Yes, union government. How is it that the union government goes further, and that the leaders of two other groups are called in to be told things they are not supposed to repeat to other members? It seems to me if those gentlemen were imbued with a real democratic spirit, if they had not the soul of Mrs. Lot, who was the victim of her curiosity and was changed into a pillar of salt, they would have told the government: This is public business, and we alone shall not be told what it is; every member of the house has the same right as we have to be told the whole thing, and we invite you to have a secret sitting for general information of members of parliament.
If the hon. member who now leads the opposition, who represents the county of Peel, and who, outside of politics, is a personal friend of mine, sits in the house, it is not at all in the capacity of leader of the oppsi-sition, because the leader of the opposition is an absentee; he is not a member of the house. If the hon. member who leads the apposition in the house has a right to use his desk, or to write a note, it is because he has been elected by the constituents of the county of Peel, as I have been elected by the people of Temis-couata, and all other hon. members who sit in this exclusive gathering have been elected by their own constituents. Therefore it is only in his capacity as a member of parliament that the government can call upon the leader of the opposition to inform him about secret matters. Yet the Prime Minister invites him, to the exclusion of all of us; and I may add that two other group leaders are enjoying favours from the government. I am reminded of Kemal Pasha who, in Turkey, chose his own leader of the opposition; and he was considered a very great man-both of them. Is it not a humiliation for the leader of the 
official opposition, and for the leaders of the C.C.F. and New Democracy groups to be considered by the government as pets who can be trusted when no other members can be trusted? I regret that my hon. friends, those leaders, have not shown a spirit sufficiently democratic to tell the government that all the members of the house should be informed about what has been going on overseas.
What about the Canadian Army? It is a veiy great thing. If Lieutenant-General McNaughton retired from the army because of his personal illness only, it is a very sad event, but it is the departure of one man only. But if he resigned on a question of principle, then we have a right to know.
Last year I spoke about a man who had sold the same coat three times. Nobody was scandalized; it was considered very smart. Then, what about the disaster at Bari? We have to know about that. We have to know who was responsible for the lack of protection for a convoy of allied ships carrying supplies essential to the 8th army and 5th army. Who was responsible for that? Nobody cares to know. I said that at five o'clock yesterday afternoon, but no one supported me. No one seems to be interested in that disaster, one which is probably responsible for the slow advance of our troops on Italian soil. I have revealed no secret, but I have tried to help hon. members not to forget certain essential matters.
I had occasion to discuss Lieutenant-General McNaughton at a time when as a civilian he was head of the national research council. But as soon as he took command of the army, as a loyal Canadian citizen I did my best to give my support to him, so far as I could. Last year when I asked why he had not been promoted to the rank of full general, I was told, in parliamentary language, to mind my own business. What is the use of having insignia for full generals or field marshals when they are not used? Whatever may be the disagreement between the Minister of National Defence and Lieutenant-General McNaughton in respect of military tactics, I express the feelings of many people, if not of many members of the House of Commons, when I suggest to the government that at last it should give him his full generalship, something he deserves, for the work he has done in creating an army now being dismantled.
I do not wish to quote the minister incorrectly, but if the British authorities did not ask Canada to send part of our troops to Italy, and if he undertook upon his own responsibility to send them there, against the advice of the commander in chief of Canadian

War Appropriation-Army
forces overseas, then it was a tremendous responsibility. It will be up to hint to explain to us why our troops should suffer from the destruction of a whole convoy in an Italian port.
I leave the matter there. I do not wish to monopolize the time of the house, and I shall give hon. members the opportunity to say all they may wish to say. But in these matters let them understand well that they cannot complain about the government, and then make themselves the instruments of the Department of National Defence as it is now. There will be no reform unless they come out of the abstract and point their fingers to the reforms that are necessary. That is something which has not yet been done. I hope theii remarks will be constructive and that they will tell, if not the government, then the committee where the reform of a bureaucracy shall begin. I am sick of the pronunciamentos of the Tory leader, who is stating his policy everywhere-"We will do this; we will do that." How will he do it? What will be the work of his party in the House of Commons to improve the Department of National Defence? If someone is to be fired, who is he? Let them say that, or not speak about reform at all. How often, when I complained of certain people, did I see the previous leader of the opposition rise in his place and complain that I was attacking faithful civil servants. He was speaking the same language as the minister. I want reform. But I cannot bring it about alone. I need some help, and there are other members who need some help. If hon. gentlemen opposite have not the support of the leader of the opposition, let them rise and make their suggestions just as I do, and then we shall get somewhere. I do not say that in any unfriendly way. I say it for the good of the country; I say it for the protection of the soldiers, and I say it for the winning of the war.

Can the minister now
answer the question I asked yesterday with reference to the calling up of boys of eighteen from the schools of Toronto for active service?

I have looked up the
order in council, and the proclamation under which the age class in fixed designates:
.	.	. every man who was born in the year
1925 . . . and all such men are required to Eubrnit themselves for medical examination and report at a military training centre or district depot to undergo and perform such military training, service or duty . . . but men born in the year 1925 shall not be served with orders-medical examination until they reach the age of eighteen years and six months.
This is an order in council that was passed on the recommendation not of the Minister of National Defence but of the Minister of Labour. In a word, they are required to submit themselves for medical examination and report at a military training centre, but until they reach eighteen years and six months they cannot be served with orders-medical examination. In the case my hon. friend mentioned was the boy under eighteen years and a half?
Eighteen years and two months.
Under the order in council they were not required to serve him with an order for medical examination.
Do I understand that boys just over eighteen are subject to call for examination?

No; they are not subject until they reach eighteen years and six months. The proclamation designates those born in the year 1925, some of whom might be just eighteen years of age, but then it limits it by saying that no one shall be served with an order for medical examination unless he is eighteen years and six months of age.
Is a boy who comes within that age class and is attending a collegiate institute or university allowed any exemption to continue his educational course?

Yes, but he is liable to call at eighteen years and six months unless he comes within certain provisions of the national selective service regulations with respect to education. I have not those before me, and I cannot give my hon. friend the exceptions or the privileges which are permitted to boys who are continuing their education. I could bring them down here, or I could get them and send them to my hon. friend.

I rise to support the hon. member for Davenport in this matter. I have frequently during the past two years raised this question of calling up boys of sixteen, seventeen and eighteen who are attending school. The time has come to call a halt on this practice, because it is disorganizing the whole school system of the province of Ontario. I do not say that the matter is altogether in the hands of the Minister of National Defence. He seems to be answering on his estimates questions -which belong to selective service, the navy, and the air force, ns well as to the army. But as a humble representative of the city of Toronto, on whose school board I served. I must say that

I should like to make a few remarks with reference to the observations of the hon. member for Broadview and the hon. member for Davenport. I assume that this discussion is really not in order, because it relates rather to national selective service regulations than to the Department of National Defence. I think I know the situation in Toronto pretty well, and I am astonished that the hon. member for Broadview is concerned about a disruption of the educational system in Toronto. He cited the leading public schools there as being affected. I know of no eighteen or eighteen and one-half year olds that are in the public schools unless they are mentally defective. The public schools are not affected at all by the order which calls for men of eighteen years subject to the draft. They are not called until they are eighteen years and six months old.
So far as the situation of the university of Toronto is concerned, I have studied it very carefully, and I want to congratulate the government upon the system which prevailed up to this year. All faculties except arts trained in the Canadian Officers' Training Corps, the university training companies. The engineering faculty is not subject to the draft. They take their basic training in the university companies but they cannot enlist without consent. So far as the medical profession is concerned, the hon. member for Parkdale knows the system which prevails under the medical procurement and assignment board, whereunder students are very grateful to this university for the opportunity extended to them of joining the army medical corps while they are taking their medical training at the university. They are getting paid around, I believe $75 or $80 a month, which enables them to pursue their studies, and immediately after their intemeships are enlisted in the army medical corps. I want to congratulate the government up.on the arrangement which was made.
So far as the arts course is concerned the system prevailing is this, that all the students take their basic training in the university
War Appropriation-Army

training companies. Those who are successful in their examinations are permitted to complete their full arts course, that is three years pass course or four years as an honour course in political science. Those who fail in the commencement examinations have their names submitted to the mobilization board and they are called up for service. Could there be any fairer system? In other words, what earthly use is there to permit a student who is a complete failure at the examination to go on at the university, perhaps to fail again the next year? I think he could do his duty far better in some branch of the services.
The hon. member for Broadview talks about competition at the universities. So far as the training companies are concerned, there is no competition at all at the university of Toronto. We have a Royal Canadian Air Force training company, an army training company, and a naval company. The students are given the option of joining any of the services. For instance, my boy, who is in his third year at the university of Toronto, has joined the Royal Canadian Air Force company and is taking his training, which will enable him to gain sufficient knowledge to expedite his initial training at the school.
In my opinion the statements on this matter made by the hon. member for Broadview are very much exaggerated. I have heard of no complaints. There may be the odd pupil in the high school who is somewhat backward at eighteen and one-half, who is still in the high school and is subject to the call; but so far as my experience in the city of Toronto is concerned the system which prevails was one of the best.
I want to say a word about the new regulations. I have seen them only in the press, but I have heard some objections to the regulation which lays down that fifty per cent, I think, of the successful pupils may continue their courses. It is said that the university authorities are going to have great difficulty in administering that regulation. I suggest to the government that this phase of the problem be reviewed.

The hon. gentleman is altogether wrong in his statement as to what I said. I did not refer to those of eighteen years in the public schools. I myself went to the public schools long before he lived in the city. What I said was that the public schools had cadet corps which had existed since confederation. The hon. member knows that; for he was on the board himself, and he knows that in the riding of ward 4 there used to be a parade of public school cadets, several thousand of them, down University avenue on

Empire day. But unfortunately the cadet services were abolished about 1937 when the pacifists got control of the board. The hon. member has been in the air force and may be out of touch with local school matters as they are to-day, but I may tell him that there are many young people getting into the secondary schools at fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen and eighteen. This is true of the collegiates in his own riding and of many other schools in the district where he lives.
What I object to is this. The cadet services were under the board of education in former years; they were there from confederation until 1937. In 1942, however, there began a duplicate practice of outside cadet corps, to which I strongly objected, as did some of the trustees. These new cadet corps officers were forming separate corps in the schools with drill after school and week-ends, and parades on Sundays, usurping the usual work of the school, physical and military. These children were taken out and put into an organization to which the government contributes $25,000, a private cadet organization, the government supplying the uniform and paying for these young people for two weeks at summer camp. All this has been done over the head of the board of education and over the school board. I object further to this duplication of services. We should leave the schools alone. Hands off the public schools and the secondary schools in the province, and the same goes for the separate schools. De La Salle has one of the finest cadet corps in Canada. Why not leave them to fulfil their own functions? Some amendment should be made to take care of these young people of fifteen, sixteen, seventeen and eighteen who belong to school cadet corps and are getting physical drill, sports and military training in the high and public schools. We should leave that work where it belongs. There are too many recruiting officers for the 'teen age students. Mr. Busybody and Mr. Highbrow have been urging these new cadet services. It is a pity they go into the schools and interfere with the young people, getting them into the air force or the army or navy too early to play on sporting teams, and I have heard complaints about this matter.
I do not need any lectures from the hon. member for Spadina. Thank goodness for that. Far from it; I was here before he was and I shall be here long after he has gone. I do not say that in criticism of the hon. member because he and I have been friends for years, but he has been away at camp, where he has done good work, and has missed some of what has been going on in respect to education in Toronto. Evidently he does not

know much about the duplication of the service and the interference in education to which I refer. At any rate, he does not know as much as he used to know, because I used to see him once in a while at the parades on University avenue when he was on the board. In the old days, at the time of the South African war and again in the great war, these young school cadets were the backbone of the militia in Toronto, and we would not have had the trouble we have to-day if the cadet movement to which they belonged had been fostered.

There are two matters to which I wish to call the attention of the Minister of National Defence. The first is with reference to the 13th Canadian Infantry Brigade, particularly in relation to the expedition last summer to Kiska. Before dealing with the matter that is on my mind, may I say in passing that we in Winnipeg are very proud of the part played in that expedition by the reconstituted 1st battalion of the Winnipeg Grenadiers, which was part of that brigade. As the minister knows, a great many of those included in the brigade were home defence or N.R.M.A. personnel. Credit should be given to them-and this is a chance of offsetting some of the remarks made in this house-by reference to their part in a dangerous expedition which might have resulted in serious losses if the Japanese had not left just before these men arrived. It should not be forgotten that even though the Japanese had left, owing to mines that were left behind there were casualties in the landing, and there were also casualties because of the kind of landing that was made in view of the expectation that it was a real invasion that was being effected. The point I wish to discuss relates to something which it might be said concerns another department, but I am told that this matter has been passed back and forth from one department to another, and I feel that it is the concern of the Department of National Defence to protect the interests of the men. I refer to the income tax deductions from the men in the 13th Canadian Infantry Brigade during the time they were in Kiska.
I asked certain questions on the order paper the other day and they were answered in Hansard of February 11, 1944, on pages 399400. These answers simply confirmed the information which had already been communicated to me, namely, that these men while in Kiska were taxed under the terms of a rule that is to be found on page 75 of the 1943 office consolidation of the Income War Tax Act. On page 75 one will find, under schedule 1, section 3, rule 3, provision for exempting 100-38
service personnel fifty per cent of their tax when serving in places in the western hemisphere other than in Canada. It is under this rule that these men were taxed while in Kiska. My contention is that they should have been taxed under the provision found on page 12 of this office consolidation. As I see it, the appropriate section on that page would be section 4 (t) (i), which is supposed to grant full exemption to personnel on the strength of overseas units outside the western hemisphere. I would point out first of all the geographical fact that Kiska is outside the western hemisphere. When I asked that question on the order paper the other day, whether Kiska is outside the western hemisphere, the official government answer was no; but according to the Encyclopaedia Britan-nica, Kiska lies between 177 and 178 degrees east longitude-in other words, two or three degrees beyond the line that geographically divides the western from the eastern hemisphere.
My information is that the answer to that question was based on the fact that there was a jog in the international dateline, and Kiska is in the western hemisphere.

858, of Hansard for 1943. He was discussing the changes that he was proposing in the income tax regulations with respect to service personnel. One sentence will make my point clear. This is what he said:
Because of the way in which the war has developed I think it is reasonable to make a distinction between those who are in the United Kingdom or elsewhere across the ocean and those who are in Newfoundland, the West Indies, Labrador or Alaska.
The point the minister was making at that time was that some consideration should be given in the light of the circumstances, the dangers and the conditions under which the men were living or fighting at the time. He was trying to keep away from previous distinctions which did not seem fair. The spirit of the exemption provisions in the Income War Tax Act should certainly apply to men who went as far as these men went, who ran the risk of suffering casualties, as they did, and of enduring hardships, as they did. The spirit of this provision should be made to apply in this case, and I have already tried to point out to the minister it seems to me a case could be made for giving them full exemption even under the letter of the Income War Tax Act as it stands at the present time; because the Income War Tax Act, when it. speaks of the western hemisphere, makes no reference to a definition of the eastern or western hemisphere. Apparently that had to be found afterwards. I repeat, the intent of the act was surely to provide special consideration in income tax matters to men who went overseas to Britain, Europe, Italy, et cetera, and it should apply to the men who went an equal distance the other way in the war against Japan.
The fact that these men were sent out of Canada is underlined by the necessity of the special order in council P.C. 5011, dated June 18, 1943, which provided for authority to the Minister of National Defence to dispatch N.R.M.A. personnel not only to the territory of Alaska but to the Aleutian islands as well and other United States islands adjacent thereto. The provisions of the N.R.M.A. were such that in order to send home defence personnel to Kiska a special order in council had to be passed. I can assure my hon. friend across the way that I am not complaining about the passing of this order in council. I feel that complaints can scarcely be registered even with regard to the passing of the order in council after the men were away from British Columbia. I have heard protests registered in that regard. But after all, as the order in council itself says, such a decision could not be made public; for if such had been done it would

War Appropriation-Army
have given information to the enemy. But I am quoting the order in council to emphasize the fact that these men were sent beyond the shores of Canada, for the defence of Canada. I repeat, they went a considerable distance; they suffered casualties; they endured very great hardships during the months they were there, and it is only fair that they should be given the full exemption. I hope the minister wilt make a further effort on behalf of the men to see what can be done in this connection.
There are other islands beyond Kiska. One never knows what plans may be arranged, or what they may call for in the way of further expeditions to the next island or to islands farther on. Just where is the line to be drawn between the men who get fifty per cent exemption and the men who get one hundred per cent? It seems to me to be quite a question. I feel that it is perfectly in order, both in the spirit and in the letter of the Income War Tax Act, that these men who went to Iviska should be regarded as having gone over the line into the eastern hemisphere.
I said there were two matters that I wished to draw to the attention of the Minister. I should like to say a word or two about the second one. It relates to the problem that arises when men are discharged from the services at their own request on compassionate grounds and find that they are some considerable distance from their home or wherever they may have to go. I have in my hand correspondence relating to a particular case, that of a naval rating, which I took up with the Minister pf National Defence for Naval Services, who of course pointed out to me that the regulations affecting naval ratings were the same as those affecting men in the other services, so that I feel it only right I should raise the question now, while we are discussing general matters relating to national defence. I would point out to the minister also that the case I have before me was brought to my attention by a former solicitor of the city of Winnipeg who is now living in retirement in Victoria, but who is doing voluntary work for the Navy League of Canada. It was in connection with his work out there that this case was brought to his attention. He wrote me about it, feeling that while this man had been looked after on a charitable basis some effort should be made to change the regulations so that this sort of thing would not happen again. In this case it became necessary for this rating, because of the condition of his wife's health, to return home to London, Ontario; but when he was discharged at Victoria he was given only S59.ll. of which $35 was the allowance 100-38J
for clothing, leaving him $24.11, which was all the money he had to get back to London. This man was looked after through the kindness of the Navy League of Canada.
Did he have a clothing allowance?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes, of $35; this was before the allowance was increased, and he was instructed that this money should be spent for clothing.
He was discharged where?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He was discharged at Victoria on his own request, because of the condition of his wife's health. She was in London; Ontario. As I say, this case was taken care of charitably, but that is hardly a desirable situation. I know other hon. members have drawn similar cases to the attention of the minister, and I repeat that I took up this matter with the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, who pointed out that to make any change in his department would require that a change be made in all three services, and he went on to mention our good friends of the treasury board. So I bring this matter to the attention of the minister in the hope that he may give some consideration to an endeavour to change the regulations so that this sort of thing may not happen again. When it is said that men are discharged at their own request, sometimes that language implies that the onus rests entirely upon the man; yet the very fact that, as in this case, the navy agreed to the request for discharge indicates that in their opinion it was justified and in fact necessary. In such cases it does seem to me that a man should not be left stranded, as this rating would have been in Victoria but for the kindness of the Navy League of Canada. I would appreciate it if the minister would say something in reference to the two matters I have drawn to his attention.

Taking the last case first, I do not think it has been brought to my personal attention before, but I am instructed that whatever the regulations were they have been amended, and provision has been made that a man is discharged from the depot at which he enlisted. I do not know whether or not there is any catch in that, but I assume that the man to whom my hon. friend refers would not have enlisted in Victoria.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is exactly the point; this man enlisted in London and was discharged at Victoria.

This will not be of much comfort to him, but if he were to be discharged under the present regulations he would receive transportation to London.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If I may just press the point a little further, the letter I received from the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services was dated February 7.
I beg pardon; I am talking about the army.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But the minister's colleague tells me that the same regulations apply in the navy.

I am told not. Here is a copy of a memorandum on the regulations which states that an officer or soldier of the Canadian army on discharge therefrom is entitled to transportation and travelling allowances as shown hereunder, except as provided in paragraph 2. If he was residing in Canada immediately prior to becoming a member of the forces, he is entitled to transportation and travelling allowances to the place in Canada where he was residing immediately prior to his appointment or enlistment. I cannot tell my hon. friend how long that has been in force.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In case I did not get it straight, may I ask the minister if this applies when a man is discharged at his own request?
I just looked to see, but I understand it applies whether or not he was discharged at his own request; there is no limitation in the regulations I have before me.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What is the date of that new order?

My hon. friend is talking about a man in the navy, and telling me that the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services said the rule in the navy was the same as in the army. I do not like to give evidence which is not in line with that of my colleague, but the information I am given is that in the army the man is discharged at the depot at which he enlisted; in other words that he is given transportation home.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That being so I shall bring this case to the attention of the minister by correspondence, and we will see if we cannot get the naval department in line with the army.

That is a change in the army regulations; it has not been so always. Now with regard to the matter of income tax for the Kiska force. I must say to my hon. friend that I have been impressed by the same considerations he has urged, and at present the matter is under serious, active consideration, meaning that it is not settled by any means at the present moment. I think my

hon. friend has put the case correctly; that is, whatever authorities there are on these matters suggest that geographically Kiska is outside the western hemisphere, but, as my hon. friend says, politically it is within the western hemisphere. By that they mean that Kiska is a possession of the United States; the United States says the island is in the western hemisphere, and we think we ought to take the statement of the country which owns the island as to what hemisphere it is in, since there is no overriding authority in the world, that I know of to argue that it is not. That is the reason for the ruling that has been given. That is in reply to my hon. friend's argument, which he has put very clearly, with regard to the question of whether or not Kiska is in the western hemisphere.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister will recall, of course, that I pointed out that the Income War Tax Act gives no definition of eastern or western hemisphere. Surely, the United States government notwithstanding, our income tax authorities have a right to decide what constitutes the western and eastern hemispheres.

They have the right to decide, but I think it is fairly good practice to take the evidence of the country which owns the island, and which says it is in the western hemisphere. So far as I know there is no one who should know better, unless it is some resident of Mars who is altogether outside the discussion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The boys who have been there know.

And of course a resident of Mars would be a very appropriate person to decide this case. The point that impressed me was the point which has also impressed my hon. friend; that is, the matter of the engagement of this force in active operations. In addition one must consider whatever weight may be gained from the fact that it was a very long distance from home, even though politically it may have been in the western hemisphere. Do not let my hon. friend misunderstand me by thinking that I am making any pledge or promise that any exception will be made to the present ruling. What I am indicating to my hon. friend is that for some time I have been interested in the same thing. Notwithstanding the fact that it is not my department, as I said yesterday I regard these men as being to some degree wards of the Department of National Defence, and that we certainly ought to do whatever we can to see that they are dealt with justly in a matter of this kind. I have not done with it by any means.

Mr. MoDONALD (Pontiac): Mr. Chairman, I have two or three questions I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence:
1.	What counties in the province of Quebec are comprised within military district No. 3, with headquarters at Kingston, Ontario?
2.	What number of men in these counties have enlisted for service overseas?
3.	Are those men reported officially as having been recruited in Quebec?

The answer to the first question is that the counties in Quebec which are included in military district No. 3 are Hull, Gatineau, Pontiac, and Temiscamingue.
I am sorry I cannot give an answer to the second question, and I do not know whether it can be compiled. However, I shall see if it can be.
The hon. member asks the number of men from those counties who have enlisted for overseas service. He will know that a request for that information is made often. The hon. member for Broadview has asked for it repeatedly, as it applies to Toronto, and I do not think that information has been given. The compilation of the numbers of men from any particular counties would require an enormous amount of work. However, I have made a note of the question.
The third question was as to whether the figures for enlistments from those counties are included in the report of recruitment for Quebec. The answer is no; the figures are not compiled by provinces, but rather by military districts. These men are shown as being recorded in military district No. 3.

I thank the minister for his answers. My questions have been prompted by the fact that certain hon. members on the opposition side of the house are making it a point to use what they call official figures in an attempt to prove that Quebec has fallen behind in enlistments. As the representative of Pontiac I am in the unfortunate position to-day of not being able to stand in my place and1 say that so many thousands have been recruited from that county. But I can say, officially or unofficially, that in proportion to the enrolable population of men in my county, enlistments have been in as great numbers as in any other county in Canada.
Figures can be used for any purpose. If the background is not given they can be most deceiving. I recall that during the last war a certain parliamentary correspondent put a question to a gentleman who was then much in the public eye. He asked for a direct yes
or no, because, he said, "Figures lie, and liars figure." In the present instance, if the figures are accepted as official they are not in accordance with the facts.
I do not wish to impute motives to anyone, but to me it is a source of deep regret that the people of Pontiac and of other adjoining counties in Quebec should be described here as having sent practically no recruits. This argument is directed particularly against French-Canadians. I represent a county which is seventy-five per cent French-Canadian; and again, having regard to the enrolable population I have no hesitation in saying that those French-Canadians have done their full duty so far as enlistments are concerned. It must not be forgotten that in Quebec we have many families in which there are great numbers of children. If I may refer to myself as an example, I am the father of ten children. Of these only one is of military age, and I am proud to state here-and I am not boasting-that he is overseas doing his duty. There are hundreds, maybe thousands of families in my county in which there are from ten to fifteen children. In many of those families none are of military age, and in others only females who are not supposed to enlist have reached that age.
When it is said that French-Canadians do not enlist I. know that such is not the case. I hold in my hand a picture of six young men of a family of nine sons. Their father, Mr. Guertin, is a messenger in this building, and those boys are all serving overseas

French-Canadians, all of them. The last to enlist was only eighteen years of age, and enlistment in the navy had been previously refused him. As a member for the county of Pontiac I feel it my duty to state in this chamber, publicly, so that statement may be placed on the record, that the men enlisting from those counties of Quebefe, comprised within military district No. 3 with headquarters at Kingston, Ontario, are not so officially reported. Nevertheless the young men from those counties have done their full duty.
About Christmas time the sad news reached a mother in my home village that her son had been killed in Italy. Four of the five boys in that family are now overseas. Yet there are hon. members in the house and others outside who try to make people believe that the French-Canadians in Quebec are not doing their duty.
I have before me an article which only recently I clipped from a newspaper, headed with these words, "Last Letter of French-Canadian Soldier Hero". This article is from
War Appropriation-Army

Arthabaska, the representative of which constituency is not in the house this afternoon, and is as follows:
Arthabaska, Que., Jan. 31.-A farewell message from their son, received several months after he had been presumed killed in a flight over Italy, is cherished by Sheriff and Mrs. Maurice Maheu of this town. It is a simple but feeling story of courage, loyalty and patriotism.
The letter is from Sergeant Francois Gabriel Maheu, a member of the French-Canadian Alouette Squadron of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
On June 28, 1943, on his thirteenth raid over Italy he failed to return and in due course was officially presumed dead. Sergeant Maheu was twenty years of age.
Some months later his farewell message was received by his parents.
"When you receive this letter," he wrote, "do not grieve over my fate. I shall already have given my life for all of you whom I love so much and for my country."
I would ask the members of the Bioc Populaire to take particular note of this, that the only thought of this young French Canadian serving in the air force was to give his life for his country. I continue the quotation.
"You will have nothing but pride and honour that one of your sons has died for the shielding of his country.
"I offer my life and my sufferings to God to make up for all the trouble I may have caused you. I have made mistakes in the past, but I repent with all my heart. Rest assured that my thought has always been with you and that it will be with you until the last moment, because from day to day I have thought of what you have been to me, and never will I be able to prove all of my affection for you. The sacrifice of my life alone, in order to assure your freedom, will be the price of what you have done for me.
"I have no money to leave you. My bequest is faithfulness to duty."

With regard to the income tax levy against the men in the Kiska force, there is this further feature, that the United States declared Kiska a combat zone, and also that these men went there to fight, and not to act as garrison troops. There is considerable concern about the matter on the Pacific coast. The ruling already made is based on a technicality, as to which there is much doubt, and I suggest that the troops be given the benefit of the doubt.

That was really the point "that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made, I think, that it was a theatre of war and a combat zone, and I myself have taken that fully into consideration. But it did not need to be declared a combat zone. I think it was one without any question at all.

There is a matter on which I should like some clarification from the

minister. I refer to order in council No. 5830, passed in August, 1941, and conferring certain wide powers on the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) with respect to the use of troops, militia and so forth in a given situation such as strikes, lock-outs, and so on. The order in council is lengthy and I shall not read it. It puts the Minister of Munitions and Supply in a position where, if he anticipates any disturbance, he may requisition troops from the Minister of National Defence merely by asking for them.
Having first exhausted the possibilities of using the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

The order in council does not state that.	It states that they may be
utilized too.
In addition, I notice that the Winnipeg Free Press of February 10 has an article headed "Stream-lining policy adopted for the Reserve Army" and it sets out five or six points, the third point of which refers to supporting the civil authority responsible for law and order, if required.
What I want the minister to clarify is this. I have seen considerable of this kind of action in the past, where the civic authorities lost control of the enforcement of law and order in a given area and requisitioned troops in the regular way, and the community or province that asked for the aid of the troops to maintain law and order had to pay the cost of the maintenance of the troops.
You mean, the bill was rendered.

Yes. There were, I agree, times when it was not paid. What I want to know is just where the Department of National Defence fit into that picture. You might have a jittery kind of chap as Minister of Munitions and Supply; it may not be the present minister. The civic authorities somewhere may wire him, "We anticipate trouble here"; then without any consultation or investigation he may, under that order in council, requisition troops from the Department of National Defence, and according to my interpretation the Minister of National Defence has no alternative but must give him the troops required. I want to find out how much control the Minister of National Defence has under that order in council with respect to the sending of troops, and in the event of troops being sent into an area for the purposes stated in the order in council, who pays the cost of maintenance of the troops in that area?

War Appropriation-Army

I have not the order in council before me. It was passed in July, 1941. I am surprised to hear my hon. friend say that the order in council does not contain a provision with regard to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I thought it did.
No.

The order in council was passed for the purpose of preventing the possibility of destruction of our war effort, particularly in respect of the production of armament and munitions. My hon. friend will remember that a very serious situation did arise with respect to the production of aluminum, at a time when that material was exceedingly scarce, exceedingly valuable and very much needed in the allied war effort, and it took some weeks to repair the damage that was done. It was felt that this was not a situation which could be imposed upon the attorney general of the province, who would not have the same information as the federal authorities would have with regard to war necessities and any emergency which arose. Obviously, the Minister of National Defence would not be fully acquainted with the conditions of production and the effect which any disturbance might have on that production. It was therefore considered that the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who, under the Munitions and Supply Act, is responsible not only for the actual production but for the planning and the maintenance of that production, was the one in the best position to assess the situation and determine whether or not it was necessary to have the assistance of troops in order to prevent a disturbance.
I am still wondering whether my hon. friend has read the order in council carefully; I am sure he generally does read things carefully. At all events the practice is that the Minister of Munitions and Supply, finding a situation which is getting out of hand and which requires assistance in preserving order which cannot be furnished by the local authorities, applies to the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is only after the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police indicates that they are not in a position to supply the necessary constables or officers to take care of the situation that the Minister of Munitions and Supply has the right to call on the Minister of National Defence to furnish troops for that purpose; and that is the authority of the Minister of National Defence to send troops to the particular area.
Answering my hon. friend's question, the Minister of National Defence himself under
the order in council is not, perhaps, called on to exercise any discretion in connection with the matter. If he refused he would assume a very grave responsibility, in view of the fact that the governor in council has placed upon the shoulders of the Minister of Munitions and Supply that responsibility. At the same time, I know the committee will believe that the Minister of National Defence, by consultation and such examination or such verification as he can make without in any way questioning the authority of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, endeavours to assure himself as far as he can that the step which is being taken is a right one and is necessary under the circumstances.
My hon. friend referred to the militia and to the announcement which had been made as to the role of the reserve army'. The role of the reserve army, as my hon. friend knows, is as old as the reserve army of the N.P.A.M. They have always been subject to be called in aid of the civil power, and that is exactly what the paragraph which my hon. friend read means. There is no addition there at all. That is what it is intended for. I suppose there might be a case when the reserve army itself would be called out under this order in council to which he has referred, with respect to the production of munitions. That has not been used, as far as I remember, in connection with the reserve army.

I am not quarrelling with the purpose for which the order was intended when it was passed in 1941; in that particular situation perhaps it was necessary. But I am rather loath to approve an order in council that gives to one minister the amount of power and latitude, with respect to the use of troops as police, that this order places in the hands of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I think the time has come when there should be a reexamination of that order, because if it is maintained in its present form in the future it can be used for other purposes than those for which it was intended. My object in bringing the matter up is to focus the attention of the Minister of National Defence upon it so that there may be reconsideration of the desirability of maintaining it in its present form in the future.

I will take note of my hon. friend's remarks, as a member of the government rather than as Minister of National Defence, because as Minister of National Defence I must recognize that the order in council is there. As I say, it was passed for a particular purpose, and having regard to the possibility of situations arising
War Appropriation-Army

which are contemplated in the recital. With deference to my hon. friend, I feel that the Minister of Munitions and Supply is the one in the government who is best qualified, and perhaps the only one qualified, to speak of the seriousness and the extremity of the emergency which calls for the exercise of these powers.

May I again refer to the question of payment of income tax by the troops who served in Kiska? I am inclined to agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I thought he presented his case fairly and logically and with due emphasis. From the remarks of the minister I take it that he had been giving this matter consideration even before the question was raised in the house. When the amendment to the Income War Tax Act was passed providing that men who served outside Canada but in the western hemisphere should pay only half the income tax, I do not think it was ever contemplated that men who were going into a battle zone should pay half; I think at that time it was contemplated that any man going into a battle zone would pay no income tax. My recollection is that when that section was added to the Income War Tax Act, places such as Newfoundland and Bermuda were in the minds of those responsible. For instance, soldiers in those places are beyond the borders of Canada and in some places, particularly in Newfoundland, they are under greater hardships than in Canada itself. I think it was in those places, Newfoundland and Bermuda particularly, that it was contemplated that soldiers would pay half income tax.
With regard to Kiska, it was always my understanding that Kiska is not in the western hemisphere. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated that geographically it was not considered to be in the western hemisphere, but politically it was.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: By the United States.

By the United States, he said. He did not know and I did not know when it was declared by the United States to be in the western hemisphere. That declaration may have been made since this war started. I do not think this government should be bound by a declaration of the United States which had been made for political purposes as to the location of Kiska.
High political purposes!

I
said, "political". I did not intend to say

"political 'purposes' ". I do not think the word "political" has anything to do with party; I think "political" is used to distinguish from "geographical".
In my view the government should take into consideration only the fact that these men were expected to go into a battle zone, and they should be given the same consideration as any men who are going into a battle zone in any part of the world. I trust the government will see fit to give them full exemption from income tax payment. The payment of income tax for the year 1943 has not been finally adjusted. No doubt a certain percentage of their pay was deducted, but the final return has not been put in, and I suggest to the government that it be made abundantly clear that when they put in their return for the year 1943 they will be allowed full tax exemption.
Mr. MaoINNIS: I should like to refer for a moment to the question raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and to ask the minister if this order has been invoked at any time since it was passed. The date, I believe, is July 9, 1941. Has the Minister of Munitions and Supply requested that troops be sent into any place where there was trouble, or anticipated trouble; have troops been sent into such location; on how many occasions, and to what places?

I have in mind that on
one occasion a requisition was made, but I do not think the troops were moved at that time. I have not the record here, but I believe that is the only occasion.
For the benefit of the hon. member for Cape Breton South I think it is well to put this order on the record. My hon. friend missed something in the order. It is numbered 5830 and dated July 29, 1941: I will not read the heading, if my hon. friend will permit Hansard to include it:
At the Government House at Ottawa
Tuesday, the 29th day of July, 1941.
Present:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council
Whereas the Minister of Justice reports that in order to insure without interruption the flow of supplies and munitions of war and the construction of all defence projects it may in some circumstances become necessary to authorize the Minister of National Defence to call out and employ the Active Militia to prevent or suppress riots, disturbances of the peace or other actions likely to impede or obstruct the production or delivery of munitions of war or supplies or the construction of defence projects;

(2)	In any case where a riot or disturbance of the peace or without limitation by the foregoing any other action whatsoever occurs or is anticipated as likely to occur which in the opinion of the Minister of Munitions and Supply threatens to obstruct or delay the production, transportation, storage or delivery of munitions of war or supplies or the construction, remodelling, repair or demolition of a defence project, the minister may request-
I call this to the attention of the committee.
-the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to take such measures as in the opinion of the said commissioner are necessary to prevent, suppress or terminate such riot, disturbance or other action as aforesaid, actual or anticipated, and the commissioner shall take such measures accordingly.
(3)	If the municipal and provincial police forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police available for the purpose are, in the opinion of the commissioner-
Not the minister.
[DOT]-inadequate or ineffectual to prevent, suppress or terminate such riot, disturbance or other action as aforesaid, the commissioner shall immediately notify the Minister of Munitions and Supply accordingly.
(4)	Thereupon the Minister of Munitions and Supply may notify the Minister of National Defence of the circumstances aforesaid and the Minister of National Defence shall thereupon issue a direction that the active militia take such measures as may be necessary to prevent, suppress or terminate such riot, disturbance or other action as aforesaid and the active militia shall take such measures accordingly.
(5)	The officers and men of such active militia when so employed, shall, without any further authority or appointment, and without taking oath of office, be held to have and may exercise, in addition to their military powers and duties, all the powers and duties of special constables, so long as they remain so employed, but they shall act only as a military body, and shall be individually liable to obey the orders of their military superior officer.
