There is a penal provision having to do with those who attempt to obstruct or delay the transportation, storage or delivery of munitions and supply. Then there is the proviso:
Provided, however, that, a person shall not be guilty of an offence under this regulation by reason only of his taking part in or peacefully persuading any other person to take part in, a strike.

I wish to refer for a moment to a subject which I raised earlier in the afternoon. It intimately affects the welfare of our armed forces and might therefore, I believe, be appropriately dealt with for a moment at this time. I refer to the subject of venereal disease. In order to indicate at the outset that, in asking the question, I had no desire to cast reflection upon any particular location in Canada, I would simply say that the whole subject was raised at a conference in Montreal in the early part of this week, as reported in the Montreal Star of Tuesday, in which Major-General Renaud, the officer commanding military district No. 4, made a statement with reference to the seriousness of venereal disease which was affecting the forces stationed in or around Montreal or who were passing through Montreal. I am aware that the defence department established, a little over a year ago, I believe, a venereal disease control department which since then has been doing excellent work under the direction of Lieutenant-Colonel D. H. Williams. I understand that the other services have each an officer associated with Colonel Williams to take care of the work in their respective fields. Since that time there has been a great improvement in the incidence of venereal disease in the three defence services. On the other hand, there has been a steady rise in the incidence of venereal disease among the civilian population, and it will be quite clear to everyone that this must also be controlled or the efforts of the army will be unavailing, because obviously the source of disease is in the communities in which the soldiers reside.
I had intended asking the minister if he would make a statement, but he has indicated his intention of doing so later on with regard to the whole venereal situation as it affects the army. I think it very desirable to call public attention to the situation that prevails throughout Canada in many communities, because it is only in this way that any cleaning-up will take place.
After I received to-day the telegram to which I referred earlier in the session, I telephoned to the chief venereal disease officer, Colonel Williams, and asked him about the situation in the city of Quebec, and he gave
War Appropriation-Army

me this interesting information, that the municipal authorities there had recently closed the various bawdy houses and that-five days after that action had been taken there was a reduction of fifty per cent in the incidence of venereal disease in the forces in that area. Therefore Quebec may very well be an example for other communities in Canada to follow.
Toronto.
I mean Quebec city, in this respect, at any rate. I am sure the members for Quebec city will be pleased to have me make this statement.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: All these stories are not about Quebec city; they are about Montreal. The hon. member read the wrong paper.

About what city? The
stories I referred to a moment ago in the early part of my remarks were about Montreal. Mr. POWER: I beg your pardon.

My statement referred to the holding up of corvettes because of the prevalence of venereal disease. Perhaps the minister did not hear that statement made earlier in the day. I made an inquiry in regard to that situation and the chief venereal officer gave me the reply which I gave a moment ago.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question? Does the telegram infer that venereal disease is among civilians or workers on these corvettes or among members of the navy who would be taking the corvettes out to sea?

If I may, I shall read the telegram:
Monday's papers state service civilian conference reveals corvettes delayed sailing Quebec through prevalence venereal disease my son volunteer for navy goes there Sunday imagine our and other parents' feelings. What is being done re situation.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Vessels could not leave Quebec in the winter anyway. We do claim there is winter navigation out of Quebec, but I think it is only theoretical; therefore I hardly think the vessels would be leaving Quebec. In any event I think the ice probably had more to do with it than the disease.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I did not want to interrupt the hon. member for Parkdale, but I believe that this discussion should take place under item 5:
5. Personnel. Supplies and services:	food,
medical and dental stores, clothing and personal equipment.
Yesterday the Minister of National Defence and the acting leader of the opposition mentioned the fact that it was difficult to keep 
the members of the committee in order on the general discussion. I want to follow implicitly the lead the committee will give me with regard to discussion under this item. We have had a general discussion for pretty nearly a week, and I believe the temper of the committee would be to pass item 1 in order to proceed with the other items. I do not want to curtail discussion in any way, but I should like to make the position clear.

Mr. Chairman, you say that this discussion could very well take place under item 5. Item 5 deals with medical and dental stores, it is true, but it does not say anything about medicine, disease or anything else. It is difficult for the committee to know just what item the different matters should come under.

I do not blame my hon. friend for finding it difficult. I must confess to the committee that if this item is taken in the broadest sense almost anything in the Department of National Defence could be discussed thereunder, because there must be civil salaries or wages paid to clerks in connection with this matter as in others. To this I have no objection whatever, Mr. Chairman. In the first place let me say I appreciate your difficulty in endeavouring to keep the committee in line in questions and discussion on the various items. The hon. member for Parkdale began this discussion, and I for one am only too pleased to have him continue it. I intend to say something about the subject this evening, if I may, because it seems to me there are many things important in the army and in the armed services, and this is one of the most important. With your consent, Mr. Chairman,
I would suggest that the hon. member for Parkdale continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Just one moment. I wish to make the position very clear. I followed quite closely the remarks of the leader of the opposition yesterday afternoon. As the committee knows, this is really not an itemized summary, but it was accepted last year. I know you will appreciate my difficulty in trying to synchronize items and so on. It is not my desire to stop discussion.

As a member in uniform I think I should intrude on this discussion.
I had not intended saying anything on the minister's estimates, but the hon. member rises in his place and makes a statement which may be used by Lord Haw Haw and Doctor Goebbels in German propaganda that the Canadian navy could not put to sea out of Quebec because it was riddled with venereal disease. I say that is a shameful thing. If

War Appropriation^-Army
it is true, the hon. member should have gone to the minister and given him that information rather than alleging all across the country that the Canadian navy could not put to sea because of venereal disease. It is a shameful thing.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. I think this is a public question and one that could very well be ventilated here.

This
is the proper place to ventilate it.
Get the real facts.

An allegation is made that
may mot be borne out at all.

We shall know what the
facts are very soon, when the minister for the navy replies to my question.
Why put it on the records of parliament until you know?
The fact remains, Mr. Chairman, that the country is very much disturbed about the increase in the incidence of venereal disease.

That is a very different
matter.

Therefore I think it is a
very proper matter to call to the attention of the committee at this time, because it may seriously interfere with the efficiency of our armed forces. If allowed to become rampant, it certainly will interfere with their efficiency. If the excellent work that is being done by the venereal disease control department is to be a hundred per cent effective, or nearly so, then it is necessary for the various communities throughout Canada to do their part by closing bawdy houses, as I believe has been done in Montreal and Quebec. I await with interest the report of the minister on this subject, but should like to call the attention of the committee to the way venereal disease has been handled in other countries, particularly in the Scandinavian countries. The incidence of syphilis in Denmark has been reduced to -2 per thousand and in Sweden to -07 per thousand.
What is Sweden doing in this war?

That is to say, one Dane in five thousand suffers from this disease and one Swede in 14,000. In twenty years they have been able to cut down venereal disease in these countries to the status of a rare disease. I believe that this should stimulate our people to greater activity in the hope that we may be able to stamp out this serious disease in this country to a very large extent.

I do not intend to occupy
very much time. I also like to get the facts.
I did not want to take up the time to put the order in council on record, but I do not interpret it as the minister does. In the first place, this order in council states that some strikes are legal. The minister will remember that under P.C. 9384, the last wage order, no strikes are legal. Therefore this order conflicts with the other.
You are not complaining about that.

I am not. Secondly, the
authority to decide whether a community has lost control of the administration of law and order is placed exclusively in the hands of the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Surely that is usurping the powers of the civic governments.
No. It has the authority to state not that they have lost control, but that the police forces are not efficient.
That is interfering with the powers which are vested in the municipalities, towns and cities. The mayor or council decided whether that situation prevailed.

I take issue with my hon. friend there. I know they have the right to decide it, they control the forces; but at the same time, where there is a federal interest, and when the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who ought to know something about the strength of the measures which must be taken to deal with a particular situation, is given that responsibility, it seems to me that my hon. friend cannot say that control is taken away from the municipal authorities. The commissioner simply appraises the ability of the municipal police force to handle the situation as it affects the federal project.

I have no objection to the commissioner doing that when he is utilizing his own forces, but I definitely do not see the matter as the minister sees it with respect to the use of troops. It is an entirely new departure; otherwise this order would not have been necessary. If in a given area, the city of Toronto, for example, or in Montreal or anywhere else, troops are necessary, it was and should be the prerogative of the city council to call them in. I think the minister will remember the last time troops were used in Nova Scotia. The town of Glace Bay refused to do what many of the other cities and municipalities did; that is, it refused to requisition the troops, and as a result they were not brought to our town. Our mayor refused to sign the requisition, and as a result
War Appropriation-Army

they were not called in. I think this matter requires an examination. The order may have been necessary when it was passed, but it contains unlimited powers which override civic powers in the matter of the use of troops. I know the minister cannot deal with the point to-day, but I merely want to focus attention upon it because it conflicts with the existing set-up. There are no more legal strikes, but under this regulation if the commissioner or the person responsible in a particular district desires to utilize the troops instead of his own forces he is at liberty to do so. Personally I am skeptical about a number of the people who are administering the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, when it comes to the question of deciding whether or not troops should be used under this order. I am not satisfied to leave that decision with them.

I was interested in the discussion that took place between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the minister with regard to an individual who was discharged from the navy at Victoria and was faced with the difficulty of securing transportation home. The minister dealt with that case as far as his department is concerned, but it happens that I, together with a group of my colleagues on this side of the house, have been attempting to study these matters in order to enlighten our own minds as to what is actually being done with regard to the demobilization and rehabilitation of the men and women in our armed services. Accordingly I thought it might be profitable to give hon. members the information we have been able to obtain in regard to such cases. I think hon. members and the people of Canada generally will be very much interested in securing full information as to the policy of the government in this regard, and it is our duty to give those who are interested all the information we can. So, that, if the minister will correct me in the event that I am wrong, I propose to put on record just what is done now with regard to a person who is discharged from any of our armed services. He is given a clothing allowance of $65, which is a decided improvement over the amount mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in connection with the individual he was discussing. In addition, the man is allowed to retain certain articles, such as underwear, shoes et cetera. He is also entitled to a rehabilitation grant consisting of one month's pay, with the dependents' allowance continued for that period, and finally he is provided with transportation and travelling expenses-

That is on discharge?
[Mr. Gillis.l
Yes.
Only one month's pay.
Yes, one month.
No matter how long he has served.

Well, of course I am dealing with what the defence department is doing. The man will be entitled to certain other things when he comes under the new department of veterans' affairs. I am speaking now of what happens at the time of discharge.
That is not enough.
Does that apply to those who are discharged at their own request?
The minister dealt with that, and I noticed he said that in his department it applies to those discharged at their own request; at least that was what I understood.
No.
I should correct my hon. friend there. I was referring to transportation home, which is granted to those discharged at their own request.
One of the reasons that moved me to speak was the fact that the regulation is a little more generous than even the minister gave himself credit for.

How long must a man
serve in the forces before he receives the grant of one month's pay?
I have not been informed as to the limitation of time.
He must serve six months, 3r 1S3 days.
My hon. friend should put all the information on record if he is going to give any of it.

I have not occupied very much of the time of this house so far this session, but I propose to place this information on record and if my hon. friend wishes more he can secure it or I can secure it for him. As I was saying, the department is a little more generous than the minister indicated. Not only is the discharged man entitled to transportation and expenses to the point of enlistment; at his own choice he is provided with transportation to the place of bona fide residence or to any other point in Canada that can be reached without additional expenditure. That is a rather important provision, because we all know that the point of enlistment may not be the point of residence, or where the man really wants to go. Through marriage, or for some other reason, his place of residence

War Appropriation-Army
may have been changed during his period of enlistment. So that I am delighted to learn that the department has taken that possibility into account and has provided a choice as to the place to which the discharged man may be given transportation.
Only if it is without additional expenditure.
Yes.
Would the hon. member explain what is really meant by those words, ''without additional expenditure"?

I think the statement I made is easily understandable. The discharged '.nan can choose transportation to the point of enlistment, or to a place of bona fide residence which may be farther away than the point of enlistment, or to any other point in Canada, provided that it does not entail greater expense than transportation to his bona fide residence.
But if that point is farther away it will entail greater expense.

I placed this information on record because I thought it might be of some assistance to those hon. members who are interested in these matters rather than in the mere political value they see in criticizing the attitude of the government. That was the sole purpose I had in mind, to give certain information not only to hon. members but also to Canadians generally who are very much interested in the welfare of the men and women enlisted in our armed forces.

I do not like to change the subject, but when I think of the work our doctors are doing at the head of the lakes, which includes Fort William, Port Arthur and the surrounding district; when I think of the work of Doctor Walter Hogarth, who has said that these diseases are definitely on the decrease, I think it is my duty to rise in my place and say that the doctors, both military and civilian, w7ho are attending the air force in Fort William, the navy in Port Arthur and the soldiers in both cities, have been doing a dandy job in keeping these men clean and fit. '

I wish to get some information from the Minister of National Defence, and at the same time register a protest against the attitude of the Departs ment of National Defence in calling up farmers for a second medical examination. In view of the shortage of labour in the farming communities, is it the intention of the minister to continue to call up farmers for a second medical examination, particularly when they have been classified in category "E"?
I should like to cite an example. Last * September I learned about a farmer who owned 160 acres of land. This man was married, but had to look after his farm by himself. He was called to Montreal for a second medical examination. Although he had been very busy at his farm work, he had to leave his farm and go to Montreal. It is true that the trip had been made at the expense of the government, but they were useless expenses. This man had been classified in category "E".
What is the purpose of calling farmers when we need them so badly? This man was alone, and had to look after 160 acres; yet he was called for a second medical examination, despite, his classification. Does the minister intend to continue this practice?

Once more I must explain that I do not call the farmers. I have no more to do with calling farmers than I have with calling men engaged in any other occupations. I ask my colleague the Minister of Labour, through national selective service, for so many men. National selective service provides the machinery under which those men are called up. A provision was made, one which I believe has been pretty well eliminated now, whereby men could be examined by civilian practitioners. I do not know the case to which my hon. friend refers, but I shall be glad to refer to my colleague, the Minister of Labour, what has been said, if the hon. merrier will give me the information. We may then ascertain if we have a record of what has been done. I do not know whether the man in question was examined by a civilian practitioner.
However, it was found-and it was bound to be so-that there is a difference among doctors as to whether a man is or is not fit, and as to what degree of disability he may have from a symptom he exhibits. The result was that a board of revision was constituted. This board consisted of doctors who had a knowledge of army requirements. They have worked under national selective service and, although I cannot give the exact title of the director, I can say that a medical officer from national selective service has in each district gone over examinations made by civilian doctors. A doctor will see what a layman would not see, and in this, that or the other case he might find it questionable whether a man should have been placed in category "E", o.r whether he might not have been placed in a category eligible for military service. In those instances the director issued an instruction that such men be called in
War Appropriation-Army

again, a procedure which was carried out in every province, irrespective of where it might be.
In one province I have in mind-and it was not Quebec-I saw figures which showed that of 2,100 men turned down and found physically unfit, medical revision disclosed that 700 were eligible for military service. I am not casting any reflection upon members of the medical profession; I am simply stating' a fact. It is quite possible that these examinations have been made when there was not the same general knowledge of army requirements.
If a man were called, whether or not he was a farmer, and was entitled to exemption under the act, then of course he should not have been called for an examination. On the other hand, if he was not entitled to exemption he would have to be called for his first examination. The medical director or registrar-I am not sure as to what his correct title is-who conducted the revision might quite possibly consider that the man in question had not been thoroughly examined, and might direct that he be called up for examination by the board of revision. That is all I can say to my hon. friend on the matter, except to emphasize once moTe that it has been found that this screening process, in which a reexamination is conducted, has disclosed cases on both sides of the line. Sometimes men who were overseas and who had been placed in categor3r "A" upon entering the army, have been discharged. On the other hand many more were found who, in the first instance, had been turned down by a civilian practitioner, but who later were found to.be medically eligible.
In what province was that?
It was in Manitoba. However, I am not picking it out particularly. I might have chosen Ontario, Prince Edward Island or any other province, because it was the same in all.

It would appear that under this item we are to be allowed to ask questions respecting medical subjects. Can the minister tell us how many psychiatrists are engaged in the army. I am asking the question because I know of some who have been checked by psychiatrists, and as a result have received satisfactory treatment.
I have, however, a complaint to make. In my view too many are shoved through the offices in a short space of time. The examinations are made too hurriedly. I understand there is an allotted time for each man, and I
fMr. Ralston.]
do not think that is a proper procedure. I do not know whether the minister agrees with me or not, but I believe the army would have fewer desertions if the psychiatrists had a better chance to check up on some of these men. I say that because many men in the army do not know where they are going, or what it is all about. In many cases they feel that it is not worth while, at all.
I shall not give any specific cases, but I do know of instances where psychiatrists have put these men on their feet, when a check was made, and it was learned what was required. In such instances good advice has been given. It is my opinion that psychiatrists should have more time to make their checks on the boys in the army.
I should like to know how many of those psychiatrists there are, and the length of time given to check each case. In many instances I understand the check is not made until it is almost too late. In my view it should be made when they come in or shortly thereafter.
This afternoon the minister was going to left us know about the number of psychiatrists in the army.
I am sorry that I have been busy since I left here at six o'clock, and I have not been able to get the figures. I shall have them to-morrow .

Another matter respecting the health of men in the army about which I should like to speak is the service of chiropodists. I understand that the air force is recognizing these people and they are doing good work, and I wondered what the army was doing to provide for chiropodists to look after the feet of the men. I understand that the army is trying to create chiropodists by a three or four weeks' course of their own, and that, of course, is causing dissatisfaction among the registered chiropodists in Canada.

I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend at this stage much information. From what I know from personal knowledge, the army has chiropodists; I know some who were practising in Ottawa who are in the army, and their services are regarded as not only useful but necessary. They are not taken in as officers; they are taken in as non-commissioned officers, and the men get the benefit of their services. Is there any particular question which my hon. friend has in mind?

Just the two matters I mentioned. The subject of diabetes has been referred to before, but could the minister tell us the different tests which the men have to go through for diabetes when they are taken into the army? Is there just, one test, or are they given a blood test also?

I cannot tell my hon. friend now. I might point out to the committee that this is where difficulty arises in endeavouring to cover all subjects under one item. I expect to have the medical officers here when the medical item comes up, but one can see that- there are a good many ramifications in .the organization and one cannot have all these people here at one time. I shall have that information. I just have now the statement that there are sixty-three psychiatrists in the Canadian army in Canada and overseas.
Does the minister think that number is sufficient? Is there any chance of getting any more?
All I know is this, that in addition to his qualifications as a medical practitioner, the director-general of medical services is himself a psychiatrist.

I
know that.

I do not think there is anybody who recognizes more the usefulness of psychiatrists in connection with army work, particularly personnel selection. As probably the hon. member knows, Major-General Chisholm was in charge of personnel selection before he was appointed director-general of medical services. We were fortunate in that, so fortunate that although sometimes personnel selection is in some way an entirely different branch, we felt that personnel selection should be taken over by the medical services, and it is one of the branches of the director-general's functions. I am sure that if more psychiatrists are needed and are obtainable, Major-General Chisholm will be the first one to see that they are employed.

The
reason I asked if we have enough is that I understand, whatever is the case now, that some few months ago a psychiatrist would go into one training camp, stay there perhaps a day or two days, then proceed to some other place, and then on to another point, but never at any time did he stay long enough in one place to do a job thoroughly. He did not have time to check on these men thoroughly. Perhaps he would see a man. in the training camp to-day, a man who might be moved out of there in a week's time, before the phychia-trist got back. That was not fair to the psychiatrist or to the man. Perhaps if that man had had a little more attention from a psychiatrist he would make a better soldier. All these men in the army have good stuff in them, and it is up to the psychiatrist to try to bring out the good in the men, and they are doing it. I think this is a matter which should be looked into.

My principal satisfaction
is that not only the officers and other ranks but the minister himself are getting in a state of mind where they are not afraid of psychiatrists.
There is a lot in that.

It was regarded for a while as a rather fearsome profession with a fearsome name. I did not like the sound of psychiatric tests, myself; but we seem to have advanced considerably in science in this particular war, and I have foupd, as my hon. friend suggests,
War Appropriation-Army

that the services of psychiatrists have been highly useful, not simply from a professional and scientific, but also from a practical point of view. Regarding what my hon. friend has said, I am thanking now of a reception centre where there is not a psychiatrist all the time; in that particular province he does have to move around; and I quite agree with my hon. friend that if we were able to have the personnel selection officer and a psychiatrist constantly there to consult-not in every case, because you do not need a psychiatrist in every case-it would be an advantage. I will make a note of the. matter and see whether the D.G.M.S. thinks there is a possibility of increasing the number of psychiatrists. I would agree with my hon. friend. I know the work they are doing and the size of the job, and I think that more psychiatrists would be useful.
I was glad to hear the minister say that we are not afraid of the name "psychiatrist."
I was-

We
all were perhaps at one time.
-but I am getting over it.

The
psychiatrists really take the place of mother and father of the men in the army because they are there to listen to the troubles of these men, and also of the girls, because they need such advice as well as the men.

In the course of the discussion on this resolution the minister made significant statements on two questions wrhich I think are of great importance, not only to this house but also to the Canadian people. First is the man-power policy of the government, having reference more particularly to the callup system under the National Resources Mobilization Act, and, secondly, the policy of the government in the war with Japan.
To deal first with the call-up system, it would appear from the statements the minister has made that that system is being allowed to die out. For example, the minister has shown that the numbers called up have dropped from 60,000 in the fiscal year 1942-43 to 25,000 in the fiscal year 1943-44, and in fact in the present year there have been only 19.000 called in the first nine months.
Enrolled, not called.

I am dealing throughout
with enrolment figures. That was to the end of December, 1943, and as against that enrolment about 3,000 have gone active, 6,500 have been discharged, which by the way seems a

very nigh percentage, and I would ask the minister to explain the reasons for which they were discharged; then there have been 1,500 deserters in the first nine months of the present fiscal year. That is a total wastage of 11,000. The minister announced that for the coming fiscal year 1944^45 there would be only 12,000 enrolled under the National Resources Mobilization Act; in other words, less than half of the number asked, for in the present fiscal year.

What was the last word?
My hon. friend said, "in other words".

In other words, less than
half the number that the government required during the fiscal year 1943-44. The minister told us last year that he was asking for 25,000 under the National Resources Mobilization Act and 75,000 for general service. Then he said yesterday that the N.R.M.A. army is now on a maintenance basis, that there will be no increase in the numbers in that army; that there will be about 50,000 fighting men fit to be sent overseans to fight, and that was the same figure he gave last year and the year before. As I say, he admitted yesterday that the N.R.M.A. army is now purely on a maintenance basis.
In the course of his statements on this resolution he has said further that there is an extensive feeding out from the N.R.M.A. army to different industries, agriculture, forestry, and so on, the total at present being about 5,300, which is done by a system of extended leave. Men are given six months' leave with the option of renewing it for a further six months and so on, which really amounts to indefinite leave.

That does not apply to
the N.R.M.A. alone.

No; that is quite true. But the minister said that there are 5,300 N.R. M.A. men . out on extended leave-8,000 altogether of whom 5,300 are N.R.M.A. men. If I am incorrect I would ask the minister to correct me. He said also that some men have been detailed for work in industry; in other words, they arfe not on leave-they had not that privilege-but have been detailed to go and work in an industry. I suggest to him that there will be more and more a demand from industry for these men in the N.R.M.A. army, particularly if those troops are not fighting and there appears to be little prospect that they will be doing any fighting. I think it is a reasonable forecast that a year from now there will be a force of fewer than 50,000 of these men who are fit for fighting. This means that the N.R.MiA. army is gradually

War Appropriation-Army
dropping out of sight and that eventually we shall reach the position where we have no effective N.R.M.A. army at all. This means further that Canada is getting back to a purely voluntary basis for raising troops, which means, of course, that we are getting back to all the inequalities which a voluntary system entails.
I suggest to the minister that there should be a clear-cut statement of policy on the part of the government with regard to this call-up system, telling us just what the intention is and where wre are heading. It is one of the most important questions in the whole of our war effort and we should have a more clear-cut statement from him.

I do not know what my
hon. friend means by a clear-cut statement. We are calling up men for the needs we have. What more does my hon. friend want? Will he particularize?

I am suggesting that the
government policy as it has been enunciated by the minister during the last few days shows that the call-up system is gradually being allowed to die out and that we shall be back on a purely voluntary basis.

My hon. friend wants
me to correct him. I will do so now. I will record here that I have not said anything that I know of which justifies that statement.
I should like to have a clear-cut announcement from the minister so that the Canadian people will know what the government has in mind.
I have been as clear-cut as possible.

The call-up system has a direct bearing on the second question, which is this: what is Canada's policy in the war against Japan? That is another question which needs clarification by the government. The two questions are related because the bulk of the N.R.M.A. army has been on the Pacific coast from the start and these N.R.M.A. men comprise the bulk of the Canadian forces out there. They were sent to replace active service men, who in turn were sent to Europe as reinforcements. This has gone so far that units which were raised originally in British Columbia have now been depleted of British Columbia men and the replacements are practically all from other parts of Canada. Eventually some of these N.R.M.A. men on the Pacific coast got to Kiska in a task force brigade, a special task force which went there with the Americans and which by the way made a very good name for itself. They are
now back on the Pacific coast along with two other brigades organized in the form of task forces, the three of them making up the sixth division. In the meantime, according to the United States press, some of the American troops who took part in the occupation of Kiska have been fighting in the Marshall islands, and have been partly responsible for the victories there. As I pointed out, Canadian troops are back in Canada.
The minister said on February 14, as reported in Hansard at page 466, the policy of the government in regard to the war against Japan is:
. . . that no commitments have been made at the present time as to the nature or extent of Canada's participation in the war against J apan.
He went on to say that the army recognized that there is a war on with Japan, and he made much the same statement last year. Here we have the policy of the government duly announced that Canada has no commitments whatever with regard to the war against Japan.
I did not say that.

I shall read it again:
. . . that no commitments have been made at the present time as to the nature or extent of Canada's participation in the war against Japan.

"As to the nature and extent". I want my hon. friend to realize what I am saying. I said, "as to the nature and extent". My hon. friend in the statement he made before he read the passage the second time said, "no commitments had been made with regard to the war against Japan". I said that was incorrect. I said, "that no commitments have been made at the present time as to the nature and extent of our participation".
I do not want to be unfair to the minister; I admit that he said that.
I do not care about my hon. friend being unfair. I want him at least to be direct.

Well, the minister seemed to be caring a whole lot; I do not know what is the matter with him. At any rate we can all agree on this one fact, that sooner or later Canadians will be fighting in the Pacific. There should be a clear-cut policy on this question and it should be announced by the government. We should not be stood off with a statement that we have no commitments at the moment as to just how, when and where we are going to fight the Japanese. There are certain features with regard to Canada's position in the Pacific which should be considered very carefully by the govern-
War Appropriation-Army

ment. First of all there is this fact that steadily the united nations are closing in on Japan. For example, it has been announced in the press that British troops either are now in Australia or will be there shortly. Canada, of course, has her own job of work to do in the Pacific war. I think it should be borne m mind that Canada cannot wait until the war in Europe is over before she does anything about the war against the Japanese. Take, for example, the question of what troops are to be used against the Japanese. I suggest to the committee that it is unfair to expect our men to come back after fighting and defeating Germany and then go out to fight the Japanese. After all, our army is a citizen army. When the men come back to Canada they will not be very keen about being rushed right to the other end of the country and sent to fight the Japanese. Furthermore, they are not trained for that type of warfare; they are not trained for jungle fighting or the type of fighting they would face in that part of the world.
Another side of the picture is that this N.R.M.A. army is available here in Canada. Certainly the units on the Pacific coast are trained and equipped for fighting the Japanese. Actually, as the minister admitted the other day, some of the units there have volunteered to fight the Japanese, although under present government policy they cannot be sent abroad to fight either the Germans or the Japanese. If some of these troops were sent out across the Pacific there are ample reinforcements among the N.R.MA. troops to keep the units up to strength.
Another feature is this: the minister made quite a play the other night about not wanting to send to Great Britain any troops who were not volunteers. He did not want to mix the volunteers and the N.R.M.A. men. If the government persists in that policy it means that none of these N.R.M.A. men will ever go to Europe. On the other hand, if they are sent to the Pacific there need be no reason to mix the two forces. I realize, and the other members of the committee realize that for the government to send the N.R.M.A. forces to the Pacific it would be necesasry first of all for the government to decide to do this, and then under the present policy to ask parliament for approval of such action. I believe that N.R.M.A. men should be made available for service anywhere in the world; that is my personal belief, but I suggest that the government should give further consideration, at least, to making these men available for fighting against the Japanese. These are the two questions on which I should like to

have some further information from the minister. They are of vital importance. They go to the root of our whole war effort in the coming year, and I would ask him to give us a clear-cut announcement as to what the government has in mind on these two questions.

With regard to the last question my hon. friend referred to, namely, Canada's participation in the war against Japan, I repeat, what I said before, that Canada as a Pacific power will remain in the war until Japan is subjugated. My hon. friend knows perfectly well, and the committee knows, that we cannot make any statement to him as to the nature and extent of Canada's participation of air forces, navy and army. I am not making any statement about that; my hon. friend would not expect it. I really do not see just what he is driving at. The point is that three brigades are on the west coast, as my hon. friend says. There, they have alternative roles; one role is to train for any necessity which may arise in connection with the Pacific situation; another role is to be, as I mentioned the other night, a backlog for reinforcements for overseas should the necessity arise and action be taken. Another role is-and it is a lesser role, it is true, just now, but a role which my hon. friend himself was most vociferous in advocating only one and a half years ago-for the defence of the Pacific coast.
That was quite right. I do not think the minister would question the wisdom of that.
My hon. friend has a very short memory. Now he says that these people are absolutely useless.
I did not say they are absolutely useless.
My hon. friend has suggested it-
I rise to a question of privilege.
There is no question of privilege at all. My hon. friend was suggesting that they were absolutely useless and that they ought to be sent somewhere.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a questior of privilege.
Mr. Chairman, I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
explain his question of privilege?
The hon. member rose to a question of privilege.

The question of privilege is this. The minister says that in the course of my remarks I said that these N.R.M.A. men were useless. I did not say that at all; I said just the opposite. I said that they had made a name for themselves at Kiska and I advocated the government changing its policy so that these men could be sent to fight against the Japanese. The minister has no right whatever to say that I stated they were useless.

I had a right to say what the effect of my hon. friend's statement was, namely, that out there they were useless. My hon. friend wanted them sent either against Japan or overseas. That was the effect of what my hon. friend said. I am calling his attention to the fact that they are on the Pacific coast, the place where he was so anxious to have twice as many troops or three times as many troops a short time ago.
I did not say they were useless there.

That was the effect of it; that we had better send them somewhere. I say they have that possible role of activities in the Pacific. They also have another role, as I said the other night, of constituting a backlog for the purpose of reinforcing the troops overseas should the occasion arise and the necessary action be taken.
And should the government change its policy.

They have a third role; that is, the defence of the Pacific coast, and a fourth, which is always possible for troops in Canada, namely, in aid to the civil power. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that these men are training to be used wherever they may be needed.
They are trained already.

My hon. friend seems to know a great deal more about the army than I do. I know about their training; I have reports from the general officer commanding-in-chief of the Pacific command in regard to it. If my hon. friend knew anything about soldiering, as I think he does, he would realize perfectly well that a man is never fully
trained, that in soldiering you go on and on, and that if a man does not keep on training, in a very short time he can become stale and require a good while to get into shape for soldiering again.
That is all I have to say about the Japanese situation. With regard to the N.R.M.A., my hon. friend rose to correct me when I sdid that in effect his statement was that these troops on the Pacific were useless. I did not rise to correct him when he made the statement that I had admitted the other night that the N.R.M.A. army would gradually go out of sight. I never said anything of the kind. I do not look for the N.R.M.A. men in the army to "die out" as he put it. I said yesterday that at the end of this year we shall still have about as many men as we have at the present time, which is between sixty and seventy thousand. That is a fairly sizable lot of men. It certainly does not show much shrinkage.
Does that include-

Perhaps my hon. friend will permit me to finish. As I say, that is not a very great shrinkage. And I said with regard to them, as I said with regard to the general service men in Canada, that our army in Canada is on a maintenance basis, just as the munitions and supply programme is on a maintenance basis both here and in the United States. That is what is happening all over; we have built up our capital commitments; we have formed our units; we have provided our initial equipment; from now on the maintenance is what is necessary, and by "maintenance" I mean taking care of reinforcements and wastage. I have not any clear-cut statement to make with regard to the N.R.M.A. beyond what I have already said. That is to say, we expect to get about twelve thousand men this year for the purpose of relieving general service personnel in order that they may be released to go overseas, if required, as reinforcements; and the N.R.M.A. personnel in Canada will be used for the duties we have for them here and any other duties for which they are trained and which it may be decided to assign to them. So far as I know there is nothing more to be said in that connection.
My hon. friend said something else that I did not quite understand. He spoke of N.R.M.A. men being released or discharged to industry, and he said the minister knew there would be more and more demand from industry for these men. My own idea is that probably there will be less demand from industry this year than previously. From what I hear, industry is not going so full out as it
War Appropriation-Army

was, by any means, and it is quite possible that men may be released from industry instead of more men being taken on. I did not quite follow my hon. friend's meaning when he made that statement.

I should like to mention another fact which was brought out by the hon. member for Vancouver South and which I find very hard to understand; perhaps he can explain it or perhaps the minister will clarify the situation. The hon. member said that the N.R.M.A. men on the west coast are willing to go to Europe but are prevented from doing so because they belong to that portion of our army which is made up of those recruits. I understood the hon. member to say that the government is preventing these men from going to Europe. I always understood that a recruit who belonged to the N.R.M.A. was at liberty to sign for overseas, and that as soon as he did so he became part of the active army and no one could prevent him from going overseas. I should like to be clear as to that.

I am afraid the hon. member misunderstood me. I said that at least some of the N.R.M.A. units-I think those that went to Kiska-have volunteered to go and fight in the Pacific. They did not volunteer to fight in Europe, but were willing to fight in the Pacific; but that because they would not volunteer to go and fight in Europe, therefore they could not be sent to the Pacific unless the government changed its present policy, under which these N.R.M.A. men cannot be sent abroad without the formal approval of this house. Now does the hon. member understand?
I do not understand why these men could not be sent anywhere in the world if they signed for. service in the active army.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This afternoon the minister and I were discussing, among other things, the question of transportation to the place of residence in the case of men discharged at their own request. It seemed to me that considerable confusion developed and that, as the record now stands, that confusion might go beyond this house. I feel that I should place on the record a portion of the letter I referred to this afternoon, which came to me from the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, who is now in his place, and perchance we can see whether or not there is any difference in the regulations as among the three services.
I would appreciate that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I quote from the letter I received from the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services under date of February 7 of this year:
.	.	. I may say that our Canadian naval
regulations jirovide that when a rating or officer is discharged for reasons other than "at his own request" he may be granted transportation and subsistence to the place at which he was living in Canada at the time of entry, or to his intended place of residence in Canada, if the conveyance thereto costs no more.
However, when an officer or rating is discharged "at his own request" no transportation is granted.
I call attention to this sentence:
Similar regulations apply in the other two services.
I quote further:
*In addition to this he also receives a clothing allowance to provide him with civilian clothing. The amount of this allowance was formerly $35 but was raised to $65 by a naval order passed on the 25th of December, 1943. A rehabilitation grant, amounting to one month's pay and allowances, is also provided on discharge, except m cases where the discharge is made at the rating's own request. All these regulations are general in the three services.
I call attention to the next paragraph:
I do not think treasury board would approve of a change in the regulations to provide for the paying of transportation in cases where the application for discharge was made by the rating himself.
That is signed by the minister. As I understood the Minister of National Defence this afternoon, however, he said that, under a recent regulation affecting the army, transportation is provided to the original place of residence, or in some cases to a newly chosen place of residence, even for men discharged at their own request. I should like some reconciliation between the statement that this has been done in the case of the army, and the statement by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services doubting whether treasury board would agree to such a request. I hope the Minister of National Defence was correct in what he told me this afternoon and, that being so, that the same regulation will be made to apply in the other two services.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I can only say to my hon. friend that, as to the army regulations on this or on any other point, what I say cannot be taken as against the view of the minister of that department. My impression was that the three services had the same regulation with regard to men discharged at their own request, and that transportation was not provided in -such cases. But if the Minister of National Defence now says that the army does provide transportation in those

War Appropriation-Army
cases, then that settles the matter so far as the army is concerned, and I was in error in my statement of what was army practice.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: When those regulations were changed with respect to the army, since we are dealing in general terms with national defence, may I ask whether the regulations were also changed with respect to the navy and the air force, and, if not, why not?

I shall have to answer that, because we have a solemn agreement between the three services that none of us shall put forward any recommendation for a change in pay and allowances, or benefits of that kind, without consulting the other.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I would expect that.

And if it was not done in this case, then it must be the fault of the army. This change is made effective on January 26, 1944, and appears in section 210 of financial regulations and instructions. It provides what I read to my hon. friend this afternoon, namely:
210 (1) An officer or soldier, other than one who is a member of the permanent active militia and in respect of whom provision is made by article 208 of these regulations shall, on ceasing to serve with the force or on being discharged therefrom be entitled to transportation and travelling expenses, except as provided in paragraph (2) below.
(a) If residing in Canada immediately prior to becoming a member of the force.
(1)	To the place in Canada where he was residing immediately prior to his appointment or enlistment, or
(ii) To any other place in Canada if the cost of the journey does not exceed the expenses authorized in (a) (i).

(2)	An officer or soldier who leaves the force for the purpose of joining any other of His Majesty's forces or an allied force shall not be entitled to transportation or travelling expenses.
So that exception does not cover the case of a man who was discharged at his own request.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: So far as the army is concerned it is perfectly clear that the man discharged at his own request is covered.
He is not excepted, to put it in another way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And did that request receive the approval of the treasury board?
Of the privy council, yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I take the opportunity at this time of calling it to the attention of the other two defence ministers.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In all probability it went into effect for the air force when it did for the army, unless we had some particular or very special reason against it. The Minister of National Defence has said there is a sort of agreement among the ministers that no service will give greater advantage by way of pay and allowances to its personnel. Then there is an inter-service committee. It is a very complicated matter. This interservice committee is sitting almqst constantly, and all those things must go to the committee of the three services. Normally there is a joint submission made to council and treasury-board by the three services.
I cannot say off hand whether we have adopted that regulation, which the army seems to have put into effect on January 26. But I would be very much surprised if we have not. And if we have not there must be a very good reason for our not doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
should like to make a short statement concerning a matter raised this afternoon by the bon. member for Parkdale. Let me say first of all that the hon. member endeavoured to raise this question before the orders of the day were called. Mr. Speaker, however, ruled that he would have to place his question on the order paper, and I assumed he would follow Mr. Speaker's direction and place his question on either the order paper for tomorrow, or that of some subsequent day.
I was not in the house this afternoon at the time the hon. member returned to the question he had attempted to raise earlier in the afternoon. He returned bo it while the estimates of the Minister of National Defence were under discussion, and read a telegram to the effect that corvettes were delayed in sailing from Quebec, on account of the prevalence of venereal disease. I doubt if my hon. friend was in order in bringing up the matter under army estimates, and I doubt if, strictly speaking, I am in order now in making reply to it. But I do feel that the suggestion the bon. member has made should be corrected, at least so far as the navy is concerned.
From the fact that the question was adress-ed to me I should gather the suggestion to be that corvettes could not sail because of the prevalence of venereal disease among members of the naval service. If that is the suggestion I should like to say I have been in touch in the last hour or two with those in the naval department who are in charge of operations, who direct the operations of our ships,
War Appropriation-Army

and I found that the last corvette sailing from Quebec sailed on December 26, or nearly two months ago. I also asked the operations branch whether they had any knowledge of any corvettes being delayed at any time at Quebec for the cause mentioned by the hon. member for Parkdaie, and I was informed definitely that no delay at Quebec could be attributed to this cause.
But, in order to make assurance doubly sure I instructed the operations branch to go further and to communicate by telephone with Surgeon-Lieut-Commander C. M. Kirk, who is senior medical officer at Quebec. Doctor Kirk is a medical man of mature years, a man of wide experience and, I think, of very great ability. He has been at Quebec since January 15, 1943-now more than thirteen months. Therefore he must be taken to be fully familiar with medical conditions among navy personnel at that point, at least for the last thirteen months.
The direct question was put to Doctor Kirk, the Surgeon-Lieutenant-Commander, in these words: "Were any ships delayed at Quebec because of venereal disease?" To this question Doctor Kirk replied categorically, "No".
I hope that this disposes of the suggestion, one which in a certain measure I regard as reflecting upon the navy personnel at Quebec. If that was the suggestion, I hope it is disposed of now. I wish to say that, so far as I know, neither at Quebec nor elsewhere has any ship at any time had to delay its sailing for the reason referred to in the telegram read to the house this afternoon by the hon. member for Parkdaie.

Mr. Chairman, may I thank
the minister for his statement, which I am pleased he has been able to give, in which he denies the newspaper report that evidently inspired the telegram to which I referred in the house.
