speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the point of order, the committee realizes that we are dealing with matters having to do with this war. All I have before me is the resolution covering the activities of the army, navy and air force. It was decided that wide discussion should be allowed. I have, however, on various occasions tried to confine the discussion to what is before the chair, but it has been difficult because evidently it was the committee's wish to have a general discussion,

I continue to quote:
Lengthy reports, including statistics, were submitted by representatives of the navy, army and air force, naval representatives on two occasions referring to the fact that infection of naval personnel in Quebec city twice had resulted in preventing corvettes going to sea to take their places in convoys sailing from Halifax.

May I ask the Minister of
National Defence if any steps have been taken to establish convalescent homes in western Canada? I ask because I understand that the government of Alberta offered the use of government house free of charge for the duration of the war and six months afterwards to the Department of Pensions and National Health as a convalescent home. I understand that the Department of Pensions and National Health referred the matter to the Department of National Defence. Has the minister any information on that?

I do not know that the
name makes any difference, but we endeavour
to give a name that comes more closely to describing the functions of these establishments. The army has established a casualty retraining centre, which is in the nature of a convalescent home, in British Columbia. The army has no other retraining centre that I remember until we get down to the one at Oakville, Ontario. The army has found it quite impracticable to establish convalescent homes in each province. It is felt that these retraining centres must be able to give an opportunity not only for treatment but for training as well, and it is not only much more economical but much better, from: an administrative and training point of view, as well as from the point of view of morale, to have large concentrations in a few places rather than a number of small, scattered' convalescent homes. The rule we have made is that there should be no fewer than two hundred at any retraining centre.
I want to say here that the department appreciates very much indeed quite a number of offers which have been made by private citizens to place their homes at the disposal of the department for use as convalescent homes. These offers have not been accepted for the reason that we believe, because of the overhead and lack of training facilities, greater efficiency is obtained by concentrating more patients at one point, that that is much more desirable from the point of view of the service itself and the morale of these men.

What is the size of the
home in British Columbia?
It has over two hundred. It is the Harrison Hot Springs hotel.

In the last two years some questions have been asked, when the minister's estimates were before the house, with reference to the Wassermann test. The minister said that this was under consideration. First, is the test being given to men entering the army? Second, is it being given periodically to men after they enter the army-every six months, or every year? Third, can the minister give the rate per thousand men, or on whatever basis the army keep their statistics, of venereal disease in Canada and in Great Britain? The reason why I particularly ask the question is that I was somewhat perturbed in reading British medical journals to see that there is concern in Great Britain about the increase in venereal disease. I should like to know if that has affected the rate as regards Canadian troops in Britain; if so, what steps are being taken to combat it; and are Wasser-mann tests being given to men in Great Britain?
War Appropriation-Army

I have not the figures for Great Britain. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Parkdale asked me with regard to the steps which were being taken in the army to combat venereal disease, and I said that I would make a statement. I only had an opportunity for a very few minutes before I came into the house to get together a few facts. I am not giving them to the committee as at all complete, but perhaps the committee would be interested in the activities in which we have engaged. I am giving figures only as far as the army is concerned, but I believe that very shortly statistics will be available for all the three services.
May I say at the beginning that the three armed services are determined in every way possible, if not to stamp out, at least to minimize the incidence of this disease. It certainly causes more loss in man-days than any other one cause in the armed forces, and a determined attempt has been made, particularly during the last year, and I am speaking of the whole of last year, to deal with this matter. The lid is off. We use films with the troops, and I will indicate to the committee some other steps which we take in this regard.
I wish to preface what I say with the remark that the most important factor in connection with combatting this disease is, as hon. members understand, getting at the source of infection in civilian communities. It is of no use for the army alone to take preventive or curative measures; the point is that we have to obtain the cooperation of the civilian authorities; and, as indicated in this report, there has been a marked improvement this year in that respect.
The army took the matter up in a special way-I mean, made it a separate study altogether-in December, 1942. We then procured the services of Lieutenant-Colonel D. H. Williams, whom we appointed army venereal disease control officer. Colonel Williams had organized a very successful four-year campaign in British Columbia against venereal diseases. An officer trained in this particular branch of medicine was placed in each military district with a sub-staff of other ranks who were trained specially for the organization. That is to say, it was not left solely to the regular medical staff, but Colonel Williams had divisional officers in each district with a sub-staff for the purpose of dealing with this matter. They gave attention to setting up a basic policy of treatment. Colonel Williams consulted with the national research council of the United States, with the American army, and a specialist at Johns Hopkins university, to set up standards of treatment for the

Canadian army. The ordinary treatment was too cumbersome to fit in with army activities.
For instance, the standard time for the treatment of syphilis had been eighteen months. A system of intensified treatment was instituted, which could be completed in one-third of that time. Before this programme, all gonorrhea patients had been going into hospital with a tremendous loss of duty time and cost of hospitalization. Under the new programme all patients are initially treated while on duty; they continue on duty training and, speaking generally, excellent results are obtained. There are, of course, a certain proportion of patients who do not respond to this type of treatment and who require hospital treatment and attention, and this is being provided to all who need it.
Until the system was revised, there was always the possibility of a VD.S. patient, that is a syphilis patient, missing his treatment on account of being transferred or moved from one post to another, with the result of delaying the cure and prolonging the disability, with the consequent loss of time, and, what was much more important, the possibility of a permanent disability being incurred.
Under the revised system a rigid control was put into force by a system of records and supervision, so that, wherever the man went, the venereal disease control officer at that station had notice of his arrival and of his condition, and the system of treatment was continued without interruption there.
Previously-and this answers my hon. friend's first question-as I have indicated to the committee before, a blood test on entering the army was not mandatory. That was changed and every man entering the army is now given a blood test immediately after enlistment. This afforded a means for detecting infected cases immediately and instituting the regular regime of treatment.
The result of these tests has been perhaps more gratifying than would be expected. It has shown-and I may say that the mandatory test has not been in effect very long, because we had to make arrangements with all the provincial laboratories to cooperate with us before this could be done-that less than one per cent of the number that have been tested are suffering from V.D.S. when entering the army.
What I have said indicates very sketchily some of the measures taken to improve conditions. The results are already evident. The rate of venereal disease for the army as a whole during 1942 was 38 per 1,000. For the whole year 1943 it was reduced to 32 per 1,000. This may not sound to the public like a very striking decrease, but I am advised

War Appropriation-Army
by the officers concerned that it is in their opinion extremely significant; it is a reduction of about sixteen per cent, and marks a genuine improvement in conditions.
So far I have spoken of the activities in the army. The committee will realize, however, that the real work has to be done among the civilian population, since that is the source of infection.
Steps were taken to investigate in every case the source of infection and to turn over immediately to the civilian health department the information obtained, for action by them. Obviously the problem could not be solved by the armed services alone. It was a joint task of civilian authorities and of the armed forces.
As part of the programme, close liaison has been established among the armed services, the Department of Pensions and National Health and the provincial health departments; and each of the three services and these federal and provincial health departments is pooling its resources and experience to put into effect and carry out measures worked out in collaboration to deal with the disease in the communities where it has its source.
Obviously, the major target against which this campaign was directed was the brothels and other unsavoury community conditions. There is no doubt that there has been a marked increase in the attention given to this matter by the civilian authorities, and it is hoped and believed that the records and information which the armed services have been able to furnish have given stimulus to their efforts and helped them to focus attention on the conditions which were perpetuating the scourge among the civilian population.
I have spoken here only of the activities of the army, of the one service, but I can say that the resources of all three services have been put forward as a team, with what I regard as very gratifying success.
My hon. friend asked me as to whether the Wasserman test is given again. I cannot give my hon. friend that information at the moment.
The third question which I think he asked was, what were the figures in Great Britain? I shall have to get that for my hon. friend, and I shall do so.

For a few minutes I wish to discuss casualties other than venereal. The annual army debate centres on two fundamental issues: first, our reinforcements, and, second, the use of the N.R.M.A. army, The minister has stated, and the committee will accept the statement, that the reinforcement situation is satisfactory, and that the 100-39
use of the N.R.M.A. army is also satisfactory so far as he is concerned. All I can say is that I trust his hope is justified. The casualties for the campaign in Italy came out tonight, 36,626 British and 28,741 Americans, or a total of approximately 65,400 in five and a half months. That just about equals the total casualties the British army suffered the first day of the Somme.
The point I want to make is this. We must be prepared to find the attack on the western defences of Germany a great deal tougher than anytnmg we have yet experienced, and we must also be prepared to find that the core of German resistance will be considerably toughened. It is extremely dangerous not to be prepared for these casualties, and I hope that the minister, when he says that the reinforcement situation is satisfactory, has really given great thought to this matter. I hope that he has not glossed over the most serious part of the task ahead of us.
There are two or three things which I think should be brought up at this time. The first is the immediate problem of the district depots, the demobilization and repatriation of the troops in the disposal wings of the district depots. It is one of the most serious problems facing the country to-day. There is no place where the soul of a man decays as much as where he is waiting around a district depot with nothing to do awaiting discharge. There develops a condition of anhedonia where every fatigue becomes a burden and every parade is an irritation. Furthermore, if these men are not put to work reasonably soon we shall be faced with a problem where a great many of them will not work again. I am not alone in that statement. That is the opinion of a great many people who have made a study of this very question.
I suggest to the minister that some immediate thought should be given to the establishment, possibly at one of the R.A.F. centres which will be closed, of a civilian training centre so that, instead of keeping these men in the district depot, they be sent where there will be an opportunity for them to study a civilian trade. And that should be done at once. We are up against it. This is a very serious matter, particularly in No. 2 district depot. This is one of the things that should be done immediately.
Next the minister brought up the case of a number of surplus officers. Admittedly there are a number of surplus officers. I do not know Whether it is true, but I have heard that there are 700 spare majors around Canada. That is the common story. If you have no use for an officer it is unfair to keep him with nothing to do. I believe these extra

War Appropriation-Army

officers should be given an opportunity now- I do not suggest that this should be retroactive-so that those who are willing to leave the army should not be penalized by being disallowed their bonus or army-leaving grant. That is an essential matter at this time.
There is much opposition from officers in the army who are thinking of getting out because they feel there is nothing for them to do. They do not want to leave because, if they leave on their own request, they do not come in for the bonus payment which is given to the man who is normally retired. I suggest that the minister should consider that point. That is my second point.
I' would ask the minister a question with regard to the function of certain parts of the army overseas. We have a corps with headquarters in Italy; we have a corps with headquarters in England; we have an army headquarters in England. But besides that we have a Canadian military headquarters in England. In other words, we have three headquarters in England. I do not know whether it is possible, but it would seem to me that if there is any possibility of reuniting the two corps of the Canadian army, an army set-up will be needed. If there is a chance of reuniting them, then the Canadian military headquarters in London is the fifth wheel to the coach. We could deal through national defence headquarters direct with the army and C.M.H.Q. would become for a great many purposes redundant and merely an extra establishment in connection with the overseas army set-up. A great deal of money could be saved by dealing directly with the army, because after all Great Britain is an operational field still, and if the two corps are not united we could deal dirgctly with them. That is a suggestion regarding which I would ask the minister for his opinion.
There is a third question which concerns a matter that I have brought to his attention. Perhaps it should be taken up under pay and allowances, but I bring it up here because I think it should be aired in the house. If a soldier of the Canadian army personnel is undergoing detention, after a period of six months the dependents' allowance is cut off from his dependents. We are unique in Canada in this respect. No matter how long a man is in detention in Great Britain, Australia or New Zealand, dependents' allowances continue to be paid. The situation in Canada is one of the greatest hardships that the dependents can possibly face. Through no fault of theirs the man is kept in the army gaol and their whole source of sustenance is cut off. I have seen a number of cases. I have one in my hand now and it is one of the most tragic

cases I have known. The entire family has been forced virtually to go on relief because of a misdemeanour of the husband. It was a simple act of striking a military policeman, which, of course, must be punished, but the consequent hardship imposed on the family constitutes one of the greatest injustices Canadians are suffering under the present act. I ask the minister to consider amending the regulations so that the penalty imposed on men justifiably, because of some crime they have committed, will not reflect itself on their dependents. It is extremely bad for the morale of the people at home as well as the soldiers overseas.
I had intended to bring up the question of hospital allowances, but I shall wait until the next item comes up because it is rather long and involved.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No. I shall not take more
than a minute. Last evening someone discussed with the minister the fact that in most of the depots there is an accumulation of men awaiting discharge. May I make a suggestion to the minister? My information is that it is not national defence that is at fault in discharging men. The trouble is with pensions and national health. That department is understaffed. National defence is handling the men satisfactorily, but because pensions and national health are not able to take them as they are boarded out through the depots there is a backlog piling up. Is there a possibility of using in the Department of Pensions and National Health some of the examining personnel in the Department of National Defence in order to break the jam that apparently is developing in some of the depots. That would partly solve the problem that the member for York West raised, that there is a large number of officers in the depots with apparently [DOT] nothing to do, who are considering the possibility of getting out. It seems to me that is one place where the minister might be able to use them to advantage by lending them to the Department of Pensions and National Health in the meantime. I merely offer that as a suggestion.

Item agreed to.
2. Pay and allowances, $547,256,061.

I
should like to mention a matter that has been mentioned before. I feel very strongly about this. I refer to the fact that when men are away without leave in Canada as well as overseas their wives have been getting along with the pay and allowances and have made certain commitments, and all of a sudden, without any
FEBRUAiRY 17, 1944
War Appropriation-Army
notice whatever, the allowance is cut off. It means that their children have to go without clothes and without food. If it had not been for the children's aid societies throughout Canada many of these children would have suffered and some would have starved. These people hesitate to go on relief because they feel it is a disgrace to have perhaps a husband or a son absent without leave. Some of these cases run for months. In fact, I know of one that is over a year old. That family is still being taken care of by the children's aid society. I believe that when men are away without leave some means should be found for looking after the family, giving them something to carry on with.

Does that mean, absent
without leave.

Yes, absent without leave. There are many such cases, as the minister knows. Dependents' allowances are immediately cut off. There are also cases where a husband is overseas and there is a child bom in the family here. The allowance is then cut off and the other children naturally suffer. There should be some adjustment there. At the present time the mother's allowance is cut off immediately.
I do not follow my hon. friend. I thought he was speaking of cases of dependents' allowances paid to dependents of those who were A.W.O.L.
Yes.

I think my hon. friend knows what the practice is. I discussed it last year. .The practice is that if a man goes absent without leave, dependents' allowance, plus the assigned pay, is continued for twenty-one days. If the soldier was in Canada payment then ceased. My hon. friend is right about that. Overseas the dependents' allowance board have taken advantage of a pretty general sort of section and they have felt that they could do more than that. What they do is this. When a man overseas is absent without leave they give dependents' allowance for three months. Then they make inquiries, but three months is the limit. Overseas they give dependents' allowance for three months in the case of a man absent without leave. If he goes absent without leave longer than that, dependents' allowance ceases to be paid.

What I am getting at is this. The wife at home does not know anything about the husband being absent without leave. She continues to get her cheque, but perhaps does not hear from her husband and suddenly the cheque is cut 100-39J
off. There should be some way of notifying the wife. I know it is an awfully ticklish job and something that is pretty hard to do. But the wife should be notified that her allowance will be cut off unless the husband is found, or the son in the case of a mother. I know it is something that the minister hesitates about. I do not know how it could be worked out, but there should be something there to look after the family. Does the minister understand what I mean?

Yes, it is a case of the humanities. One would not want to notify her at once because of the hope that he might turn up, or for fear she might get the idea that something had gone wrong domestically, or something of that sort, but I agree with my hon. friend that there must come a time, and not too late, when she should have some waning of the fact that this allowance is not going to continue forever. I am told that the dependents' allowance board does make an effort. I shall inquire'into it; I think it is just a human touch that might be carried out. I am not quite sure how it could be done; I think it would have to be done differently in individual cases.

Yes; each case would have to be handled separately. Then how about the illegitimate child; how about the dependents' allowance in that case, where the husband is overseas and there is an illegitimate child born to the wife? The allowance is cut off.
No; there is no allowance granted if the husband is overseas.
It is cut off.
It is not given. I understand my hon. friend to refer to an illegitimate child born while the husband is overseas?
Yes. In that case the mother's allowance is cut off.

It is not automatic; there is always an inquiry into the case. I just happen to remember that, because I had a case on my desk the other day in which the dependents' allowance board wanted to find out about the mother's reputation in the community. Representations were made by responsible citizens that the time had come when they thought the allowance should be paid, and finally the allowance was paid.

Is that done in every case now?
War Appropriation-Army

The investigation is made in every case. I am informed also that the husband is consulted; that is, if he knows about it and condones the situation, of course that is an important contributing factor.
In some cases naturally the husband overseas objects, and- then I understand the mother does not get the allowance.

I am sorry I cannot say what the board does in circumstances of that kind. I know it investigates the merits of the case, not only from the point of view of morals but from the point of view of the need, and that in a number of cases payments are made.
In some cases there are other children in the family and it works a hardship on them. The children get their allowance, of course, but the mother does not get hers.
The children, of course, do get the allowance.
Their allowance keeps on, but the mother's $35 is immediately cut off.
The other children get the allowance; that is to say the children who were in the home when the husband went away, and some increase is made in their allowance.
Not in all cases.
In some cases. It may be done; the board has discretion.
But the minister will look into the question of men overseas who are away without leave?
A note has been made of that.

I do not altogether agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Peterborough West. In the case of a woman whose husband overseas is absent without leave it seems to me a most unfair proposition that the woman who is left in Canada should be told after a while that her cheque will not be forthcoming any more. After all is said and done, if that man had not had to go to war perhaps he and his wife would have lived together in this country for many years, in fact all their lives. Many of our men who have had to live in England for two or three years now may find themselves in the position that they are seeking other companionship, and it is a terrible situation for all concerned.
IMr. G. K. Fraser.]
But I do not see why the woman left in this country should be penalized on that account. In my opinion any woman whose husband is in that position should at least receive her cheque until the war is over and her husband is brought back again, when the army authorities can find out what relationship is to be maintained in the future. It may be that these men will resume living with their wives in this country. They may not, but in the interval those women are certainly entitled to protection because this country needs their men somewhere else, in England or some other theatre of war, and they should have their cheques until the war is over.
I agree with what the hon. member has just said: I think it would be wonderful if the dependents' allowance board would do that.
But she does not agree with you.

I know that; some ladies do not agree with me. My idea was that if the dependents' allowance were not going to be continued, they should let the wife know some time before the cheque was to be stopped, and I think the hon. member will agree with that.
Quite so.
She does not want that time to come, though.
The hon. member is quite right; I agree that the dependents' allowance board would be doing a wonderful thing if they would continue the payment of those allowances until the end of the war.

When I made way for the hon. member for North Battleford I realized that she would make a much more eloquent appeal in this matter than I could, but I think we should lend whatever emphasis we can to the plea made by the hon. member and supported by the hon. member for Peterborough West. I think this is a matter to which the minister should give attention as soon as possible. I have never been able to see why, because a soldier or a sailor or an airman is absent without leave, the wife at home should have to suffer. It is not her fault; it cannot be traced in any way, directly or indirectly, to her. In our regulations with respect to dependents' allowances we recognize that while a man is away from home in the forces, this country has an obligation to look after his wife and family, meagre though that assistance may be in some instances. The principle has been

War Appropriation-Army
adopted under which she is taken care of financially to a certain extent. Surely that principle is not interfered with because of something the husband does. I could readily understand that something the wife might do would interfere with her allowance being granted, but surely we could not argue that something the wife did here should interfere with the pay of the man overseas. If that be a sound argument, then of course we ought to apply it in reverse as well. Therefore I am going to ask the minister if he will not give consideration to some change in the regulations so that the wives of those men who have gone absent without leave may have their allowances continued until the end of the war, as suggested by the hon. member for North Battleford. I cannot make that plea too emphatic at this time. I think most hon. members have had some distressing cases brought to their attention in this regard, and I should be surprised if most hon. members would not lend their support to this suggestion. I do not wish to labour the point at the moment, but I should like to impress upon the minister as strongly as possible that this is one change in the regulations to which the government ought to give immediate consideration.

I do not want to be on the defensive in connection with this matter but, as is usual in cases of this kind, it is not quite as obvious as it may appear. I have been affected in the same way as my hon. friend has by the apparent merit of a case of this kind, and it has merit. It is an appealing case; there is no doubt about that. In the first place, however, we have to come back to the theory of dependents' allowances. Dependents' allowance is not granted as compensation to a wife because she has lost the comfort of or association with her husband. It is paid to the wife in order to promote the well-being of the service, and to relieve the anxiety which husbands overseas would have, if such payment were not being made. Instead of the payment being made to him over there, he knows it is getting to her, and the provisions in the dependents' allowance regulations sets that out. It states:
A dependents' allowance may not be claimed as a right. The allowance is for the purpose of promoting the well-being and efficiency of the military forces of Canada by providing a means to alleviate the financial anxieties of temporarily enrolled members with respect to the domestic welfare of dependents while they are in the service of His Majesty.
That is the first point. The second1 point that the committee does have to remember is that if a man can just go absent without leave, not having any worries at all about his
family, then certainly there is no disciplinary effect whatsoever. He just simply goes. There must be some deterrent effect, encouraging his staying, or causing him to stay, in the service if he knows his family will suffer if he goes out. If a man could simply walk out and say, "Oh, I know the government will take care of my family anyway, notwithstanding the fact that I am not serving", he is no good to the service. He will take dependents' allowance, go absent without leave, avoid the provost corps, and his family be looked after, and he will think, "Well, I am all right."
If we take the principle the minister has now stated, are we not really using the condition in which a wife may find herself as a means of disciplining a man in the armed forces'?
No.
Actually there are penalties and regulations within the armed forces to take care of the very situation, without penalizing the wife and children at home.

No, it is not that, at all. I am saying the argument the other way is that it makes the position entirely too easy for the man, and that is not quite fair to the service which, after all, is the thing of paramount importance. If the provision were that a man could simply go absent without leave and be assured that the dependents' allowance would nevertheless be kept on for his family, it would almost be putting a premium on delinquency or at least it removes a deterrent.
There is one other feature I am surprised someone has not mentioned. I noted it a year ago. Perhaps you may think I have not worked very hard at it, or I should have had something done about it. However, there is a certain inconsistency in this respect that I never could understand. I am saying this in the presence of the chairman of the dependents' board of trustees, namely, that the wife of a man who goes absent without leave will continue to get three months' dependents' allowance at the most, but the wife of the man who is in detention will continue to get the allowance for six months. I never could quite understand why there should be that difference. That caused me to look over United States regulations, and when I have looked at the regulations for that country and for Australia, I find there is a distinct difference in those cases. The theory may be that at least it is positive in the case of the man who is in detention, that the man will come back to the army some day, whereas in respect of the man who is absent without leave he may never turn up again.
War Appropriation-Army

I wish I could promise the committee favourable consideration, but I will say that I shall study it again. It might be pointed out, however, that we in the army are just a little bit careful in considering these provisions, particularly in a case of this kind, where a man is not serving, and where he has offended against regulations with the result that we have lost the benefit of his training, and everything else that has been done for him. There is a tendency to break down discipline if one were to act too leniently in these cases. This may sound hard-hearted, because it will be said that the wife is concerned. At the same time it is for the good of the service that we are acting, and it is not much encouragement to the good soldier to "stick it" when he knows that another man can quit and still have his dependents' allowance continued to his family. However, I shall look into the matter again, to see if anything further should be done about it.
Would it not be possible for the minister to devise some way whereby the penalty would be imposed against the man?
If we could find him.
There must be military discipline which would make him feel his obligations, rather than penalize those who are at home, who are totally innocent. I cannot see the argument which has been made.
We are not penalizing. We are not supporting them; that is all.

May I add something to what has been said. I have one case in my *own constituency concerning a man who has been overseas since 1939. Possibly a year or fifteen months ago he was supposed to be away without leave. His wife received dependents' allowance for ninety days. She has three small children,, and since that time has had to depend upon relief payments from the municipality. That man has been absent for much more than a year. He has not yet been apprehended, and, as I have said, his family are now on relief. Surely he should have been apprehended in less than twelve or thirteen months. I point out to the minister that a case of that kind should receive favourable consideration, for the simple reason that this woman believes her husband may have been killed in the blitz over England, and that he has never been a deserter. Perhaps the minister might give consideration to a case of that kind.

There are one or two matters I would draw to the attention of the committee. and in doing so I agree whole-heartedly 
with the hon. member who has just taken his seat. A couple of cases have been brought to my attention in which soldiers are presumed to have deserted in England. It becomes extremely difficult for one who is probably not personally familiar with the type of organization existing over there to prevent the landing of subversive aliens and to prevent sabotage, to understand how these desertions can continue for so long. We have always been led to believe it would be extremely difficult for a man to be at large in England for a period of eight or nine months or a year, and not be apprehended. I should say a good deal of responsibility must rest upon the military authorities for a man's not having been apprehended in less than ten or twelve months.
Several branches of the legion are keenly concerned about this matter. I would ask the minister to indicate to the committee the' number of desertions presumed to have taken place in England, the number of such deserters who have been apprehended, the number who have not been accounted for, and the number who have been discovered dead either through suicide or, as another hon. member has suggested, through the blitz.
Two or three cases have come to my attention where a man, who married a widow with a family, has enlisted. For a period of two or three months that man has not been able to secure dependents' allowance. In each case he was told there was every possibility that those children were illegitimate. That is a most unfair suggestion. I am very much afraid my personal reaction would have been one leading to violence, under conditions of that kind. One soldier who came to me was extremely bitter, as a result of the officer telling him point-blank that there was every reason to believe the children were probably illegitimate. Three months elapsed before that case was cleared up.
Then the minister indicated that where the wife at home has probably not conducted herself as it is believed she should have, inquiries are made in the community. I do not know just what that implies, but I do know that in many instances it is virtually impossible for a soldier's wife to appear at a dance without having some of the community talking about it for a week afterwards. I am very much afraid that if you go into a community and try to secure an impression from some of the people there how a soldier's wife is conducting herself, you may in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred not get a very favourable impression.

I do not believe anything of the kind. I do not agree with that at all.

War Appropriation-Army
I would have moved if I lived in a community like that.
I base myself on a case in the district of Red Deer.
My hon. friend bases his statement about ninety-nine people on one particular case.
That is not fair at all. I said to the minister that I would refer to one case that comes to my mind. I am not basing my assertion on the one case at all.

If my hon. friend will permit me, I want to take issue with him at once when he states that in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the reports given by neighbours about a soldier's wife would give an unfavourable impression.
This will make nice reading in England.
I do not believe anything of the kind. I think it is a slander on the wives of the soldiers.
It is a slander on the whole community.

I am not particularly impressed by the remarks which I am hearing because they are improperly interpreted. I was a bit concerned when the minister said that we can go into a community and make inquiries. Why should the minister not be more explicit? If I am wrong as to the type of inquiry that is made, I am the first one to admit it. But in cases of this kind where a wife is accused perhaps of not conducting herself as she probably should, I ask, what type of inquiry is made? Who carries on the investigations and what constitutes proof? If a soldier disclaims paternity of a child, do they accept that as evidence? I have a case where that was done. The soldier simply refused to claim the child and the mother has been deprived not only of an allowance for that child but of the separation allowance also. The soldier is stationed within approximately eighty miles of where the home is located. Would the minister comment on the situation with respect to desertions in England?
Mr. RALSTON I have not the figures here. I do not think I should give the figures with regard to desertions in England and the number apprehended; I do not think it would be in the interest of the state to give them. I am sure it is a very small number compared with the desertions in Canada, but I do not think it is a figure I should give in the house. I do not mind giving it to my hon. friend or to any other hon. member privately.

The whole question of pay and allowances for the forces overseas introduces one aspect about which I should like to say a few words, particularly since the question of soldiers serving detention is linked up with it.
I have had an opportunity to see and interview a considerable number of soldiers under sentence for military crimes, to some extent in this country, but more so on the other side.
I wonder if the minister would not be inclined to agree that one of the strong contributing factors to habitual delinquency in the forces is the system of pay deductions, under financial regulations and instructions which have been adopted almost holus-bolus from the British army, and which, so far as I am able to discover, go back to pre-Wellington days in some respects at least, when soldiers were regarded hardly as citizens of the country but were pressed-men and, generally speaking, were less . well regarded than they are to-day.
I am satisfied from what observations I have been able to make myself and from conversations with senior officers in the service, particularly in the army, that the problem of habitual delinquency in the army ties up with the system of pay deductions. It is possible for a soldier to go absent without leave, let us say for purposes of illustration, for fourteen days. When he is apprehended he loses his pay for those fourteen days. If he is sentenced by a court-martial, as he is likely to be, if his desertion takes place in the field, he may be fined some additional days pay as part of his punishment, and of course he loses his pay during all the time he is undergoing his court-martial sen-fence. I do not suggest for a moment that a soldier who, having made a contract with His Majesty to serve in the forces, deserts and fails to perform his duties should be paid for the days he is absent. I do not suggest that a soldier who is punished by undergoing detention, during which time he is unable to perform his military duties, should be paid during the period of his detention. But I do think that some more modern and equitable system could be worked out in the interests of the service itself than the present system under which the soldier, when he has served his sentence and expiated his crime in that manner, comes out of detention owing considerable sums of money so that when he begins to draw pay again he can draw, if he is in England, only thirty shillings a month, whioh is scarcely enough for cigarettes if the mail is held up, as it often is. And so, finding that he cannot hold up his end with his fellows he commits some army crime again, perhaps steals a pair of army boots or a tin of butter, knowing full

well that he will get it in the neck if he is caught, as eventually he must be. I interviewed in England' one man who lost 1,191 days' pay for army crimes, and he deserved it. This war will not last long enough for him ever to get what he owed .paid) off.
If a soldier commits a civilian crime to-day and he is apprehended by the civilian authorities-I know one man who served twelve months in Wormwood Scrubs, which is a rather unpleasant prison-when he comes out he may properly be charged1 with being absent without leave; being absent as a result of a felony; and, if he is sentenced to serve an additional ninety days by court-martial, that would cause him some further financial difficulties. So that the man who embarks on a career of army crimes is considerably handicapped in his chances of reform by the present archaic system of pay stoppages. I do not wish to labour that point. The minister and the department are fully aware that many highly placed personages in the army, who have never been in detention and are not likely to be, are not sympathetic to the present system and feel that a system more in the interests of the service itself could be devised.
There is another type of thing which I would mention, not as a criticism, but simply to bring it to the attention of the authorities with a view to a remedy being found which would be to the improvement of the service. I know a man personally who at the time he enlisted stated that his wife was his common-law wife and that he had lived with her and supported her for two years, and that as such she was entitled to separation allowance, and he also made over to her assigned pay. About the time I went to England last fall his legal wife, having discovered that he was in the service and that the government might be approached with a view to assisting her financially, did make such a request. I understand that the request was turned' down; that she then attacked the arrangement with the common-law wife, on the basis that they had not lived together for the required period of time and that consequently, in this particular case, they had received the assigned pay and separation allowance fraudulently. An investigation was carried on-I am sorry I am not able to say by what agency it was carried on -but I understand that the approach as to whether or not this chap had lived with his common-law wife publicly as such, was made through the near relatives of the man himself, and if so, I am not surprised that they should deny the allegation, since he comes from an exceedingly good family who are very proud of their reputation and would not condone such a thing.

In any event, what I began to take exception to was that, when this sergeant was brought before his commanding officer, under instructions, he was informed that he, having received separation allowance for his common-law wife for a period of two years or thereabouts, obtained it fraudulently, and now owed thirteen hundred and some odd dollars which he would have to pay back out of his share of his pay. When I investigated this matter-(I can give my hon. friend the name and the particulars if he wishes, but I choose not to at the moment)-a little further, as to whether it would be possible to waive.this sum already in excess of $1,300-I was told-not by a member of the government, for I have not brought it to the attention of the department, since at the moment I only want to use the episode to illustrate the inequities of the system-that it was no use, that nothing could be done about this because the government could not condone a fraud, and could not forgive the money he owed, so that consequently nothing could be done about it. And this, even though I pointed out that in 1936 it was established as government practice that with regard to a pension received fraudulently or in error, while it could be stopped, there could be no recovery. The man did what I think I would have done, although I think I would have done it better than he did. Under those circumstances, with a load like this around his neck, and reduced to the ranks, realizing that this war will not last long enough to enable him to pay back this money, and that he could not soldier on thirty shillings a month, he "went over the hill". He did not make a good enough job of it, because he was subsequently arrested, and at the time I last saw him was undergoing a sentence. When he comes out of detention he will have an additional load of financial debt, and his situation is increasingly hopeless. The man was an excellent sergeant. I am satisfied that he made the contract in good faith, and even if that could not be established, I think that a system of stoppages, which permits that type of penalty to be hung on that man, after a period of two years, a man who as a soldier must have cost the people of Canada $3,500 as an absolute minimum to train to be an efficient sergeant; a man who to-day is and for some months to come will be in detention and lost to the service, simply does not make sense.
While we are on this subject of detention and of people who are absent without leave, I might remark that there are people in England belonging to the Canadian army who have been absent without leave longer than

War Appropriation-Army
twelve months, who have not been apprehended, who have not been blitzed, and who, indeed, have been occupied1 in lucrative positions in civilian life during that time, I know of one case which I may cite by way of illustration to allay the fears of my hon. friend here, of a young lad who "jumped ship" in the city of Halifax. He joined the Canadian army and was sent overseas shortly afterwards on a draft. When he got overseas with the draft they said to him, "You are too young to fight; you will have to wait-" I think it was a year at 'that time, or a year and one-half. He had been a sailor before; so he went to London and soon got a job on a merchant ship, and for thirteen months he plied the seas. He was at Dunkirk, and he was in and out of the Mediterranean a number of times during that period. He came back to England to visit his parents and they said to him, "You plan to go to Canada after the war. What kind of future will you have as a deserter? Give yourself up." He went to Canada House to give himself up. They said, "Go away; you are crazy"; they would not believe him. Finally he convinced them, went back to camp, asked to take some courses when in camp, but he could not get them, and decided that he might as well fight at sea until he was old enough to fight on land. So he went away for eleven months, and then again surrendered himself formally to Canada House, did his punishment for being absent without leave, and did it proudly, because he carries from the shipping authorities a very fine record of service at sea. He was, as I said, at Dunkirk, in the Mediterranean and to Russia; he has seen more war than most of our senior officers, or for that matter anybody else in any army. The last time I saw him he was waiting to get out of the "clink" to go to Italy, where I expect he is to-day. I hope he survives to come back to Canada, because he is the kind of man we need.
I have not said this to condone absence without leave but to illustrate the fact that it is not particularly difficult to get away and be away for long periods of time. The English people are very hospitable. They treat our boys very well. They treat them too well. You can live longer in England without money if you are absent without leave than anywhere I know of-and you do not have to-swim the Irish channel to find security, as was suggested to us sometimes in the last war.
If we are concerned about the problem of army crime, and I think we are, we ought to adopt a system of pay stoppages a little more in line with the sort of equity we hand out in the courts in Canada andi as they do in 100-40
other countries. I suggest to the minister that if he wants anybody or anything to strengthen his hand when he puts this matter before the military council, I know where he can get somewhere between five and six hundred cases to establish for him the cumulative effect of pay stoppages as one of the great influences in making fellows into habitual army criminals.
On the subject of army criminals I have had some experience with cheeky young fellows who have had detention time after time. When I was engaged in the job of salvaging some of these fellows, most of whom are young lads, one of them remarked to me that he did not have any great consciousness of sin. I spoke to him firmly and inquiringly, with a straight face. I said, "What are your crimes?" He said, "They are all absence without leave." I spoke to him of the seriousness of that. He said, "I have a brother a little older than I am. He has been trying to get into the army for four years, but he was an automotive worker, and he cannot get into the army because they will not release him from the plant where he works in Canada. He is living comfortably at home, making good money. If he gets drunk on Sunday night and doesn't feel like working Monday and doesn't go back until Tuesday, the boys there simply say, 'I guess Bill is working out his income tax'. So there he is, nice and secure at home. I am a volunteer. It is not my fault that I was not killed or wounded three years ago. Yet if I take a day off I become a criminal." That argument does not make sense, and you cannot control an army on the basis of condoning that type of thing. But when you come to examine into why a lad like that takes months off and he feels he is not a criminal when he does that sort of thing, I think you will find, back of a great number of these so-called habitual cases, the fact that he went "on the loose" two or three times and came back in debt.
In the case of every man in detention whom I have had an opportunity to examine, I have demanded particulars, and got them from the commanding officers in every case. I have asked, "How much money will this man owe when he comes out of detention?" And the number of men whom I found that would not owe money-I am talking about married men-I believe I can count on my fingers. When a married man deserts and is caught and punished, not only the separation allowance but his own assigned pay are paid to his wife for a period not in excess of six months. We continue to pay $20 a month to his dependents in the case of a private. I differ a little from some of my friends, who see no reason why we should not continue

War Appropriation-Army

to pay to the family even though the man has deserted. I conceive it to be the responsibility of the government, when it takes a man out of his job, away from his family and his environment, and puts him into the service, to look after his wife and children until such time as it is determined what has happened to him. But in my opinion that is not properly chargeable to the army. If a man has a, job in civil life and he quits that job, or if he goes to gaol in consequence of a felony, his pay is stopped and any contribution he makes to his family is also stopped. If the cutting off of the allowance that is given in the army is to be made a deterrent, I suggest it would be a better deterrent if the man knew that, in the event of his quitting the army in this manner, the allowance to his family would be stopped. If it is intended to be a deterrent, let us make it a real deterrent and cut off his pay the day he quits. I would not relieve the Canadian people, through their institutions, of the responsibility of looking after a man's dependents until I knew whether or not something in the military history surrounding that man had contributed to his delinquency.
Sometimes, I think, we do contribute to such delinquency by this obsolete system of pay stoppages, and sometimes we contribute by bad man-management. I do not suggest for one moment that it is possible for the Canadian people, through the government, to escape some measure of responsibility for the man's family, but I would not pay a nickel of his straight army pay from the minute he was in detention or absent without leave. If the minister wants support for that view I am ready to give that as my opinion. I would not say that these people should not be subject to care and welfare, but that is not a charge which is properly chargeable to the army, when a man has ceased to function in the army, with which he has a contract, unless it can be shown that the army has contributed to his delinquency. Sometimes that can be shown. There are cases of men who were unsuited to the service through no fault of their own. They should not have been there. There are numerous situations that enter into this question, contributing to the desertion of many men. In such cases the family would not have been deserted if the soldier had not left home, and we should treat the man's wife and family just as if he were the good soldier he promised to be when he enlisted. We cannot escape responsibility for looking after these dependents until such time as we can find out the degree to which we have contributed to the man's delinquency through our institutions, selection and management.

I appreciate my hon. friend's contribution to the debate. He has first-hand knowledge of the subject, acquired both in Canada and in England. On the first point, there are at the present time before the department certain recommendations from Canadian military headquarters with regard to the cumulative effect of charging assigned pay in respect of a soldier who is in detention.

I wish the minister could give me an explanation about the discrimination shown between the mothers of soldiers and their wives. I have no doubt the matter has often been brought to his attention, and I have applied to many officials for an explanation that would square not only with my sense of justice but with anyone else's, an explanation that one could fairly put up to the woman concerned. The soldier's wife gets S35 a month and an allowance is made for children. The soldier's mother who is a dependent gets at most $20.

Call it $25. For a long time, three years at any rate, it was $20 as against $35. Various reasons have been given me by different officials. On one occasion I was told that the same thing was done in Britain. Well, in my opinion, that is a poor reason. Another time I was told that a man had a greater responsibility to his wife than to his children. I cannot see that. Another reason was given, namely, that the wife was looking after the children. Yes; hut the wife is paid extra for looking after the children. They get the children's allowance.
Here is the point as people, as the women and as I see it. The soldier's wife is generally a young woman and she has around $70 in the way of ordinary allowances. She is able to do her own chores, her own housework, chop her own firewood perhaps, and keep a garden, and on occasion I have known them to work in plywood factories getting seventy cents an hour. But the mother is probably an old woman. She is not able to work and needs medicine, which is expensive. She needs doctoring, and that, too, is expensive. In my opinion she is in more need of support from the government than the wife, because she is less able to take care of herself.
As regards the argument that a man's responsibility is greater toward his wife than it is toward his children, the answer is this. It is not a question of responsibility; it is a question of dependency. If they are both dependent they are dependent to the same extent. You cannot make a distinction between the dependency of the one woman and the dependency of anothe-. and in fact. R takes

War Appropriation-Army
more to keep a dependent mother than a wife. I have never been able to see any justification for the principle. I have been corrected; I have been told they are getting $25 but the mother cannot demand even $25. It is at the decision of the committee. Well, why was it made $25? That was done as a belated attempt to justify the low amount that was given before. The thing is either right or wrong and $25 is not enough as compared with $35, even if the amount has been raised from $20. I should like to have something that I can tell these people who want information on the subject. They ask this question: Why do I get $25 as compared with the soldier's wife who gets $35? I have never been able to obtain from any official or anyone else an answer that would jibe with anyone's common sense and sense of justice, and I would be very much obliged if the minister could give me something satisfactory that I could pass on to these women as fair and reasonable.

I have tried several times to tell my hon. friend all I know about this, and that does not take very long. The relationship is different legally as between the wife and the mother. As a matter of fact, we have said, and have stated in the house, that regardless of the fact that dependents' allowances are not payable as of right, we regard the dependent's allowance to the wife as being payable as of right to the full amount. The mother's allowance is based on dependency. That is why what is sometimes called the means test is applied. The mother is entitled to dependents allowance up to $25. In order to get that $25 the son has to assign fifteen days' pay to her which would amount to about $23. The two together come to $48.
The mother is not entitled to demand even $25; it is only possible at the whim of a committee.

It is possible, but my point is this: if she does not establish her right or her need for $25, does my hon. friend suggest she ought to receive it. She must establish her need. She may get up to $25, but she only gets that provided the son assigns pay. There is one exception to that. I said the son assigns fifteen days' pay.
Is it the same for the wife?

If the son has assigned fifteen days' pay to his wife, he must assign an additional five days' pay to his mother in order to qualify the mother to get dependents' allowance. The reason for the difference between wife and mother allowances is that there is a different relationship. I have mentioned 100-40J
that on previous occasions. Secondly, there is the fact that the mother is put in the dependent class. But she has to show dependency, whereas the wife normally receives the $35 allowance automatically. If she were a millionaire or had an income of her own, she would still get the S35 allowance. On the other hand the mother does not get any dependents' allowance unless she is in need of it. The third point which does not apply to dependents allowances only, but it applies to pensions under the Pension Act is that somehow or another our pension people from the very beginning have always made a distinction between the mother and the wife. Under the Pension Act dependency in the case of the mother has to be shown, as must be done in the case of any relative other than the wife. It may be that that rule is wrong too, that these acts are wrong. They have been revised in this house many times, but that provision has always stood, the provision for the mother being based on actual dependency and the provision for the wife being based on need. I do not think I can add anything more to what my hon. friend has said.
How many days' pay would a girl in the army have to assign to the mother?
It is on the'same basis as for the men.
Would the minister indicate-
