speakername: @Acting Chair(man)? of Committees of the Whole

speechtext: I should like to ask one question while it is fresh in my mind. Is the dependents' board of trustees entitled by regulation to deal with mothers?

Yes, if the mothers are in receipt of dependents' allowance. The dependents' board of trustees, as the committee knows, is empowered to supplement allowances in meritorious cases, and the board is entitled to deal with mothers as dependents just the same as children or wives.

There are two things I should like to mention to the minister. I want to join with those who have already spoken with regard to wives of soldiers who are away without leave. A year ago I had occasion to have one of those cases brought to my attention. I brought it to the attention of the department, but was unable to have any satisfactory arrangement arrived
War Appropriation-Army

at in regard to that particular case. I think it is very unjust that a wife, whose husband has served in the armed forces for probably a year or two and then deserts the army, is thrown absolutely on the mercy of charity. I believe the army or the government-I will put it in that way so that I shall not get at variance with the hon. member for Winnipeg South-should pay the allowance. I do not care who pays the allowance so long as somebody does. I think the government has the responsibility in a case like that. The case that was drawn to my attention in Calgary a year ago was that of a young girl only nineteen years of age. They both agreed that the husband should join the armed forces and do his share in the defence of this country. He did it and spent about a year and a half overseas in the armed forces. If my memory serves me alight he served for nearly a year in England on active service. Then for some unknown reason he went away without leave. He was never heard of by either the army or his wife. She was left absolutely on charity, on the hospitality of the Salvation Army. She had two little children. She arranged in some way or another to have those children taken care of by one of the neighbours and she went to work. Then the child welfare authorities came around and made her quit her job and go home to take care of her children. That woman was in a terrible position. I think the government has a definite responsibility. I do not think that woman should be allowed to depend on charity. That is only one case of many that hon. members have had brought to their attention in this house. I think it would be well worth the government's while, and the minister's as well, to give this some very, very serious consideration to see what could be done. I know the minister does not like to see these cases. I am quite convinced of that. The thing is to bring pressure to bear upon those who are responsible, to alter this regulation and see if some assistance cannot be given to those wives whose husbands are away without leave.
The other matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is that of dependent mothers. I brought this up the other day. The minister said he was going to make a statement about it, but he has not yet done so. According to regulation 101, section (c), subsection (iii):
Mother or foster mother, whose husband is alive but totally incapacitated from earning a living if the officer or soldier is her "sole or partial support."
The case I brought to the government's attention just about a week ago has a direct bearing on this clause. Because of the word-

ing of the clause the dependents' allowance board takes the stand, and rightly so, that the mother is not entitled to any dependents' allowance whatsoever unless the husband is
totally incapacitated. The words "totally incapacitated" should be changed. If the father gets an amount as small as $5 a month
the mother is not entitled to dependents' allowance because the father is not totally incapacitated. I do not think that was the intention of the government; nevertheless the regulation is there, and the dependents' allowance board, interpreting the regulations, must refuse the mother any assistance. I think that is wrong. I ask the minister if he will make a statement in regard to the assigned pay in a case like this. A soldier is on active service and assigning a portion of his pay to his mother or to his wife in the hope that when he comes back he will have sufficient laid aside for him to take advantage of the rehabilitation plan whereby he can take up a farm, if he has ten per cent of the cash value to put up. He hopes that his wife or mother will take this assigned pay and put it in the bank for him and not use it as a means of livelihood. But if that assigned pay were used it would make it decidedly unfair. I do not think the assigned pay should necessarily have to be used in order to keep the wife or mother. I think the dependents' allowance should take care of that. There should be a distinction as to whether or not the dependents' allowance must be classed as income. I do not think it is clear in the regulations, and certainly there should be some clarification of the regulations with regard to total incapacitation. The minister promised to make a statement on that matter, but I suppose it has slipped his mind.

The only statement I can make is that at the present moment we have under consideration an amendment making thgt definition of "totally incapacitated" less restrictive, and dealing also with the amount of income which the mother and father jointly may be permitted to receive.
I think that is a good thing.

I should like to support the remarks of the last speaker, and also those of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I think a widowed mother who has in the armed forces a son who has been her sole support should be entitled to the same amount of allowance that is given a wife. As one hon. member pointed out, in many cases the mother is not able to earn a living as easily as a wife without children might. I

War Appropriation-Army
know of many such cases, and I trust that the minister wiH use his influence to have these allowances increased. When we discussed this matter last year the allowance was only $20; now it has been increased1 to $25, and I hope it may be increased still further. As I have said, many widowed mothers are in greater need of this allowance than are many young wives who are able to work and support themselves. I realize the force of the reasons given by the minister, but I hope he will use his influence to have the amount increased.
I should like also to support what has been said by other hon. members, that the state is responsible for the wife and children of a soldier who goes absent without leave. Certainly it is no fault of the wife and children, but in many cases a distinct hardship results, and I hope some changes will be made in that respect.
There is another question I should like to ask the minister, dealing with the case of a man who enlists at a time when there is some domestic or family trouble. His wife happens to be of a very independent nature, and he does not assign any pay or ask for the dependents' allowance for his wife and children. She goes on working for many months, but finally illness overtakes her and she is not able to keep on providing for herself and the children. Is there any means by which the dependents' allowance may be put through in such cases? I know of such instances, and at the present time these people are finding it very difficult to get along. I have one or two other questions to ask, but perhaps the minister would clear up these matters first.

As I understand it, even though the man has not assigned bis pay in the first place he may do so at any time. In addition, there is a provision under which the board in effect can bring about a compulsory assignment and give the wife the status of a dependent for the purpose of receiving the dependents' allowance.
There is no time limit?
No.

Could the minister tell us approximately what it costs to clothe an individual soldier? This has a bearing on the clothing allowance. If there is anything that has gone all out of kilter under the wartime prices and trade board set-up, it is the cost of clothing. I am sure no one would rise in his place in this house and say that to-day you oan purchase clothing of the same quality or
at the same price as when we entered this war. In order to give some comparison, I think the minister might tell us what it costs in dollars and cents to clothe a soldier to-day, because that has some bearing on the allowance given the soldier when he is discharged.

I do not think that is quite relevant. My hon. friend does not want to find out the cost of military clothing; he wants to find out the cost of civilian clothing, and it seems to me he would know as much about that as I do. The fact that a man gets a uniform, an outfit and certain equipment in the army does not prove anything in regard to the cost of getting a civilian outfit.

I think it would be well to have those figures anyway, because I have an article before me which states that clothing now costs 121 per cent of what it cost formerly, and I think the minister will agree that you cannot fit a man but for $65. A step has been taken in the right direction by increasing the clothing allowance, but it is still not nearly enough.

There is one other point with regard to the mothers' allowance that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, though probably it has been mentioned already. I refer to the ceiling that is placed upon the earnings of a dependent mother. I understand that a mother may receive up to $25, provided she is not earning more than $40 in addition.
That is $40 exclusive of the assigned pay.
Yes, so that the ceiling is $65.
Plus the assigned pay.

Yes, but that means
she cannot work at a job paying more than $10 a week. If she is to receive the dependents' allowance she must earn less than $10 a week, which in most cases means that she cannot work at all.
Oh, no; the $25 would be reduced, that is all.

She would get $15, $10 or even $5, making $65 the maximum she may receive, with her allowance. There must be thousands of mothers across the country who are supporting younger children. The son in the army is perhaps the oldest, and she has come to depend almost entirely upon, his income. I have personal knowledge of numbers of such cases, where the mother still has to support younger children. There is a
b22
War Appropriation-Army

feeling that there should be no ceiling, that the mother should be permitted to earn what she can and still receive her allowance. I am also told that the mother gets no cost-of-living bonus, which is paid to wives. I should like to know the basis for that discrimination. In the first place thie mother gets an allowance of $10 less than the wife; in the second place there is a ceiling placed on her income, and in the third place the mother is not given the cost-of-living bonus. I think that is discrimination.

Of course the ceiling
placed on earnings is because of the feature of dependency which is required to be shown in the case of a mother and which does not need to be shown in the case of a wife. The idea is that the country does not contribute if the mother is earning $65 a month; that means she is not in a dependent condition, and that is the reason. I tried to explain to the hon. member for Comox-iAIberni-I am afraid not very successfully-why there is a difference in principle between the allowance to the mother and the allowance to the wife. The one has what is not very popular, the means test, while the other has not. I think perhaps in that one sentence I have dealt with the question of the ceiling and the matter of dependency. What was the other distinction?
The cost of living bonus.
I cannot tell my hon. friend why that is not given; I do not know.
Do the wives of all members of the armed forces, except those who are also members of parliament, receive the dependents' allowance?
Yes; all wives whose husbands assign pay and who are living in the usual marital relations receive dependents' allowance.

I want to support what has just been said in regard to mothers' allowances. Although the minister has said something about it just now, I protested last year by stating that I never could quite see why a mother who is absolutely dependent upon her son, a mother perhaps with two or three children, did not come in the same category as a wife. However, I hope something may be worked out in that connection.
I should also like to support the hon. member for Souris and several other hon. members who have spoken respecting wives whose husbands have been absent without leave.

There are one or two other questions I should like to ask the minister. The first refers to a man Who has been discharged from the army, at his own request, because of sickness, or some other reason along those lines. Is such a man entitled to clothing allowance?
He is entitled to clothing allowance, but not to rehabilitation allowance.

That would seem unfair in some cases. I have in mind a man who was discharged because his wife was unable to take care of his family. Perhaps he should not have been in the army, to start with, but 'the fact is that he was in the army. I was wondering if those cases are reviewed, or if there is a hard-and-fast rule concerning it. Are they ever given an alternative?

No. My hon. friend will understand that the rehabilitation grant is exactly what it states, namely a grant for the purpose of refitting a man into civilian life. The assumption is that if he takes the option and requests a discharge, he has somewhere to go, some occupation at which he may be engaged. Otherwise he would not be asking for the discharge.

Under the circumstances, when he comes back he has to find somewhere to go. Is that a hard-and-fast rule, or would those cases be reviewed? In such cases I should think the few dollars he would get as rehabilitation allowance would be very acceptable to his family, in fact, would be a godsend.
Could he earn more monpy out of the army than in it?
He did not earn any money for a couple of months after he came back.
Why was he discharged, then? Was it just a matter of having to keep a house?
He had to come back to look after his family. His wife was suffering from a heart condition.
My hon. friend will understand that, generally speaking, a discharge at his own request is for the purpose of taking a job.

I think while he is
hospitalized.

He would be there for a considerable time, perhaps extending into a year. It seems very unfair that a man coming from the army and hospitalized is discharged as soon as possible from the army when it is learned he cannot go back to the army because of a disability. True, he will receive a small pension, but it is pretty hard on his family. Certainly he should receive consideration during the time of his initial hospitalization.
While I am on my feet may I point out to the minister the difficulty we had in connection with those soldiers who were discharged after the last war, after having received wounds. They wanted to get out of the army as quickly as possible and in leaving the army they did not care about anything. They did not find out whether anything was physically wrong with them. After the expiration of some time difficulties would develop. I have no doubt all members of parliament have had many cases of that kind to take up with the pension authorities, and we have had much difficulty in such cases. We would receive the reply, "Disability not accounted for by active service."
To-day men are being discharged from the army every day because of disabilities. They do not know where to go or what to do, and are not familiar with their rights. They do not realize that at some time in the future they may be pensionable, and may need that pension. I am wondering if a full record of the reasons for discharge is made, or whether a history of each case is kept and given to them upon their discharge, so that they will know where they stand. I have in mind the case of a young man who was supposed to be in A-l condition. Examinations, however, are not always correct because, while this man was entered in the army as A-l, it was found upon X-ray that he had a congenital deformity of the spine. This condition showed up on service.
In fairness to this man, and in view of the difficulties members of parliament have had in connection with pensionable cases, I say that the very fullest explanations of reasons for
discharge should be given to each man who is discharged.
To the men themselves?

They should also receive histories of their cases, setting hut the reasons for their disability, and the immediate cause of such disability. For instance, a man might be sent to perform duty in pouring rain, and following that might catch cold. Bronchitis, developing into a chronic bronchitis might be the result. If possible, there should be an attempt to pin it down to the reason for disability, thereby providing a full history of the man in question. Surely in fairness that is the least that could be done. I tell the minister that if such action were taken we would rid ourselves of endless troubles. Then, if a man were told that his discharge was for such and such a reason, and that he would probably be entitled to a pension, he could then be informed where to go, how to make his application, and be given all necessary details. The man would not be placed in the position where he would say, "Oh well, I will forget all about it." His disability may be a serious thing for him in future life, and it is not fair to neglect taking a full history.

The hon. member complains that in the cases to which he has referred discharges were made quickly. Then, in the last case he pointed out that sufficient information was not given at the time of discharge.
That is right; it was not given to him.

I understand that. May I repeat to the committee what I said last night, namely, that the hon. member has touched upon one of the most sensitive times in a man's army life, that is the time he is discharged. I have tried with all my power to impress that upon my officers. We have had liaison with the Department of Pensions and National Health, in an effort to have an officer from that department and one of our own officers at a hospital, or a board room, or wherever it may be, so that a soldier may be advised' of his rights, and where he ought to go. This is most important. This is one of the many things the R.C.A.F. do particularly well, in connection with their repatriated men. When they bring them back, they try to look after them. Anything that I can do to meet that situation I assure my hon. friend will be done. A case occurred quite a while ago of an officer that I found in hospital who had been discharged and had not been told either by the army or by the Department of Pensions and National Health what his rights were.
War Appropriation-Army

The case was brought to my attention imme-dately, and I saw that everything was done in order to make up for what was, in my judgment, crass indifference. We are doing everything we can to tighten that up and see that the men are given information promptly, particularly as to what their rights are and where they can go. My hon. friend is quite right in saying that when a man gets out of the army he does not know where to go next. He expects somebody to send for him, and they are apt to send for him after the papers have been signed and he has gone away.
The reason why I brought the matter to the minister's attention is that I do not think as much care is taken as should be taken. I had a case within the last month.
Is my hon. friend thinking of the case of an officer from Hamilton?

No; of two or three cases from Christie Street hospital, Toronto. I do not want to go into the details because it is not necessary. But I wish to impress upon the minister that greater care should be taken to inform the men what their rights are.
Mr. RALSTON The system is no good unless it works. I will look into it.

I have been in
touch, as many of the Toronto members have, with the pension advocates in Toronto. I know them well and they are very good men. They have impressed upon me the necessity of getting all the information out to the soldier promptly so as to save a whole lot of trouble later on.
There was another case of a man at Christie Street hospital for observation. He really did not know why he was there until he was discharged. He never was told why he was there. He was discharged, and then he came back later on for a pension.

I wish to add my voice to those that have been raised in protest against the stoppage of pay and allowances. The minister did not, I think, make out a very good case in defence of the present practice. He may have so far as the army is concerned, but from the point of view of the people I do not think he did, because in reality what he was saying was that the army is holding the wives and children of the soldiers as hostages against the soldiers' good behaviour. In the case of a soldier serving a sentence for desertion, the practice is to stop the pay and allowance at the end of six months. I do not think the minister could possibly 
defend that, for this reason: The army has the body of the soldier, and as long as it has the body of the soldier it can get enough work out of him to pay for the dependents' allowance.
The argument has been made that it is no different from similar cases in civilian life, where a man is put in gaol, and his salary stopped. But industry has not the body of the soldier. The army has the body of the soldier, and the army can get enough work out of him to pay for the dependents' allowance, or wait until he is out of gaol and then take it out of his pay. At least in cases where the soldier has been captured and sentenced to gaol, the dependents' allowance should be paid continuously.
I want to refer to article 102 (d) of the financial regulations and instructions respecting dependents in T.B. sanatoria and mental institutions. This memorandum is marked "confidential" in big type. Am I at liberty to quote from it?
Is it from the department?

Yes, a memorandum from the dependents' allowance board. It reads:
Dependents in T.B. sanatoria and mental institutions
1.	Article 102 (d) of financial regulations and instructions provides-"No allowance shall be granted to a person who is maintained in an institution at the expense of a public authority."
2.	In order that dependents who become patients of these institutions may be eligible for dependents allowance the board has an arrangement with most of these institutions whereby they agreed to accept $20 per month for the maintenance of an adult dependent and $12 a month for the maintenance of a child of a member of the armed forces.
I have in mind the cases of several wives of soldiers who are in T.B. sanatoria in Alberta and S20 a month is being deducted from their dependents' allowance and paid to the T.B. institution. But in Alberta, T.B. treatment is free, and so the provincial government are prepared to return the S20 to the soldier's dependent. But if the provincial government returns that $20 to the dependent the Department of National Defence takes the stand that they would have to deduct another $20 from the dependent. Surely provision should be made whereby the provincial government is able to return that money, because otherwise you have this peculiar situation, that while T.B. treatment in Alberta is free to the people at large, the only one who has to pay for it is the wife of a soldier. For everybody else the treatment is free. That is a very undesirable situation. The dependents' allowance

board have told me that the only way to get around it would be for the provincial government to pay the money to the dependent and not tell the dependents' allowance board that it had done so. I was not quite satisfied with that because I could not get it in writing. I then took it tip with the Minister of Finance, and he referred me to the comptroller of the treasury. I wanted to know whether the government would guarantee, that in case the provincial government returned the money to the dependent, no inspector would be sent out to try to find out if the money had been repaid. The Minister of Finance said that the comptroller of the treasury was the only person who could guarantee that, and he would not do it. When you have an absurd situation of that kind the regulations should be amended. The minister must agree that it is a most undesirable situation when the soldier's wife is the only person in Alberta who cannot get free hospital treatment for the soldier patient.

Strangely enough, a case of that kind came to my attention last Sunday afternoon when I was clearing up a few matters. There was a letter from the Hon. Mr. Cross of Alberta, making the offer which my hon. friend has just mentioned. The solution appeared easy to the dependents' allowance board, namely, that the province would just pay back to the person in the institution the amount which had been paid to the province for maintenance. I must say that I generally try to cut red tape, but I saw a little difficulty in doing that under the regulations. I immediately inquired from the board if there were not some other way of working the thing out. I am thoroughly in accord with my hon. friend's objective that we must find a way of working it out. It is a case of the soldier's dependents being discriminated against to the extent that they do not get the benefit of the provincial contribution. I am trying to work it out and I think I can do it.

Will the minister make an announcement when he has worked it out? We
have some cases pending.

I am in correspondence with the Hon. Mr. Cross and perhaps I should correspond with him first. I shall make an announcement to the committee as soon as possible.

Progress reported.
